Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. Concentrations of particles were discovered in the northern celestial sphere, specifically in the direction of the Local Supercluster, the Coma Berenices star cluster, and the Scorpius OB2 association, all of which are relevant to the origins of these particles. Additionally, we observed areas with reduced particle concentrations in the southern celestial sphere, pointing towards underdense regions in the intergalactic medium that these high-energy particles could encounter during their journey to Earth. The lack of anisotropy below 20 EeV leads us to suspect that the primary component of extremely energetic cosmic rays undergoes an important transformation above this threshold. The size, shape, and orientation of these anisotropic patterns remained stable over time, suggesting they are steady rather than transient phenomena. The anisotropic patterns themselves hold significant implications for our understanding of cosmic magnetic fields and the distribution of sources that these high-energy particles originate from. The finding that charged cosmic sources contribute more significantly to high-energy particle distributions at lower latitudes also supports the "Galamin" model of cosmic magnetism. The vast majority of these sources fall within 75 degrees of the Galactic plane. The absence of anisotropy in the northern celestial sphere above 20 EeV, coupled with the discovery of the "Galactic Wall" and associated structures, points towards a source distribution that mirrors the morphology of the Milky Way. The overall picture painted by these findings highlights complex patterns of cosmic anisotropy that reflect both the distribution of sources and the intervening cosmic magnetic fields, and stresses the importance of considering the role of the Galactic environment in shaping these patterns. The extensive nature of these anisotropies, extending over millions of light years, also underscores the importance of a multi-telescope approach in fully capturing these phenomena. This paper proves that all Zinbiel algebras are solvable. A compact and clear proof of their nilpotency is also provided, demonstrating that their lower central series terminates at a trivial element. Additionally, guidelines for creating graduate students' research projects related to this topic are discussed. Our study identifies experimentally observable effects of the sizeable initial angular momentum in non-central heavy-ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Specifically, we investigate how the distribution of flow angles and magnitudes is altered in semi-peripheral lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV through an analysis of charged particle data. Our research demonstrates sizeable fluctuations in flow angles and magnitudes, offering opportunities for testing the properties of relativistic nuclear matter and quark-globally monopole interactions. Moreover, flow angle and magnitude distributions exhibit unique polarization characteristics that can be utilized as probes of initial conditions and collective behavior. Lastly, our findings in heavy-ion collisions complement similar phenomena observed in asymmetric proton-proton collisions at the LHC.

Point processes provide a superior alternative to time series models like ARIMA for analyzing data with irregular time intervals. However, integrating point processes with time series patterns requires more sophisticated models, which have seen limited development. In contrast, point processes have been highly successful in model development, but lack the inclusion of time series data. This paper addresses this imbalance by introducing the Poisson Autoregressive model, which combines the benefits of point processes and time series models. Unlike homogeneous Poisson Autoregressive models, which have already been established, the current research focuses on heterogeneous variants consisting of a dynamic background rate and recursive coefficients similar to those found in traditional autoregressive models. This novel model features accurate forecasting capabilities and enables background rate and coefficient estimation. In addition, the paper provides four different statistical estimation approaches for testing the Poisson Autoregressive model's parameters. Lastly, the model's performance and statistical estimation methods are validated through comprehensive simulations and real-world data applications. This includes a case study on modeling traffic flow, a critical issue in intelligent transportation systems. The findings of this research have been made publicly accessible through an R package called papr.

Our proposed Neural Descriptor Fields construct object representations that include both local shapes and poses, leveraging a unique combination of a pose-dependent convolutional network and a pose-independent fully connected network. This object representation, posed in 6D space, enables efficient matching and comparison between objects, even with varying poses. Unlike other methods that employ pose-related regression, our approach determines the object's pose directly from its 3D local features, ensuring that pose and shape are distinct and independent. This is further reinforced by introducing an equivariance constraint, ensuring that the representation remains invariant to rotations. Our experiments on the ModelNet40 dataset demonstrate improved classification results, and creations of a new dataset, MixNet40, show that Neural Descriptor Fields excel in object classification with varying poses. Additionally, our results on the ABC dataset showcase the efficacy of our approach in 6D object pose estimation. The code for Neural Descriptor Fields is available at https://github.com/PRPR-UoH/Neural-Descriptor-Fields.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs when spheres enter water's surface. This surface seal phenomenon, seen in both slow-moving and high-speed water entry scenarios, involves the formation of a seal or air pocket that eventually collapses, creating a sound similar to a "splash". abstraction of previous research suggests that slower-moving water entries result in deeper air pocket formations, whereas faster-moving water entries yield shallower pockets. On the other hand, faster-moving water entries produce smaller pocket diameters. Our research involved capturing water entry events at intermediate speed regimes using high-speed cameras and microphones, and analyzing the resulting air pocket formations and sound waves. By examining these formations and sound waves, we were able to identify two distinct speed-based groups among our subjects, each characterized by unique air pocket formation dimensions and sound wave patterns. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the curvature of the water's surface plays a significant role in determining the air pocket formations and sound waves generated during water entry events. Lastly, our research also highlighted the occurrence of a less frequently reported water entry scenario known as "delayed seal", which can occur even at lower speed regimes.

Additionally, our findings suggest that the introduction of carriers can lead to an orbital-dependent mechanism of carrier scattering, providing an explanation for the anisotropic effective mass observations. Lastly, our study highlights the unique features of cubanite's electronic structure, with implications for its magnetic properties and potential for unconventional superconductivity.

The behavior of quantum systems is influenced by external fields, but even in isolated systems, phenomena like oscillations between energy levels can also occur, stemming from variability in their own quantum nature. In this study, we focus on semiconductors and look at how entangled electrons known as "dark states" behave on their own, without any external influence. The study reveals that these dark states can shift back and forth between energy levels due to internal instability, a phenomenon that can be detected by light. The light reflected or emitted during this process can take on a specific pattern, and this pattern can be analyzed to gain insight into the internal workings of these dark states. The study further reveals that the light pattern can indicate when the dark states are transitioning between energy levels, and this transition can be a massive shift, thousands of times greater than their normal movement. The finding can have a significant impact on controlling and manipulating light and matter interactions in quantum systems. The study employed a mathematical model of semiconductors made of silicon and carbon-based materials known as graphene, and the results were analyzed to understand the behavior of these dark states in isolation and how they interact with light. The analysis revealed that the light interactions with these dark states can take on a unique, complex pattern, but this pattern can be simplified by changing the internal characteristics of the dark states. The change in the light pattern due to the change in the dark states' characteristics can provide valuable information on their internal workings. The study also found that the light interactions with these dark states can cause the semiconductors' electrons to become even more entangled, a phenomenon that can be detected by light. The detection of this entanglement and the complex light pattern due to the shift of the dark states between energy levels can both occur at the same point in time, and this point in time can be determined by analyzing the light interactions with the semiconductors. The study further revealed that the semiconductors' ability to shift between energy levels and become entangled with each other can be controlled by changing their internal characteristics, but this control requires a very precise change, otherwise it can have no effect or even the opposite effect. The study finally suggests that the semiconductors made of silicon and carbon-based materials known as graphene can be used to create a device that can generate a complex light pattern due to the shift of the dark states between energy levels, and this device can also detect the point in time when the semiconductors' electrons become entangled with each other. Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice derived from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group. This lattice exhibits a 2D equivalent of a 3D non-symmorphic Weyl semimetal architecture, comprising a central honeycomb framework surrounded by two layers of hexagonal lattices oriented perpendicular to each other. Notably, this structure harbors multiple types of Weyl points, including a novel kind that has no direct 3D analog. By adjusting a potential difference between the hexagonal layers, we can manipulate the Weyl points' location and even create a "Fermi-arc" that encircles a singular Weyl point, as well as a ring of Dirac points surrounding a central "V" shape. This structure offers tunable topological properties and could be implemented using PbSe nanoscale 2D layers aligned with a calcite (104) surface. Our proposed model also has the advantage of being experimentally accessible within a real-space framework. Moreover, by incorporating spin-orbit coupling, we find that the Weyl points transform into a "monkey head" shape along the x-z plane, and the Dirac points' rings change to a "double ring" structure. Additionally, our research reveals a triple Weyl point phase that arises when the chemical potential falls within the central "V" shape, accompanied by three distinct Fermi arcs and a ring of points along the y-axis. The model we presented has the benefit of being scalable to 3D architecture by stacking the 2D lattice layers in a specific manner, offering guidance for experimental realization. The calculated electronic band structures are depicted graphically across various parameter combinations, along with the corresponding surface and bulk band indicators, and the proposed geometry is also illustrated with atomic arrangements based on first-principles calculations. Quantum states of light play a crucial role in the development of quantum communication systems. The process of quantum-optical catalysis converts an unknown input light state into a specific output state, based on detection of a signal reflected from the input. This research investigates the possibility of implementing a particular catalysis device, which produces a coherent state with a well-defined photon number when a single photon is present in the input state. The development of a corresponding quantum circuit is also explored. Furthermore, the paper examines the impact of the device's precision on the quality of the generated coherent state. The development of a strategy to determine the efficiency of the device without knowing the initial light state is also discussed. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise nature of the electromagnetic and gravitational phenomena occurring in complex spacetime environments. This review delves into the fundamental principles and detailed calculations underlying this crucial concept. Specifically, it explains how the Weyl tensor's natural decomposition into the Newman-Penrose formalism helps define the Weyl curvature index, a vital parameter in identifying the specific characteristics of electromagnetic and gravitational waves. This index, which can be determined from the coefficients of the Weyl tensor's decomposition, distinguishes between the effects of the electromagnetic force and the gravitational force, and also clarifies the distinct effects of the gravitational force, particularly general relativity, and the cosmological constant. This review also explores the relationship between the Weyl curvature index and the Einstein field equations, providing a comprehensive understanding of its physical significance. Furthermore, this review highlights the key advantages of the Weyl curvature index, particularly its ability to accurately characterize the physical mechanisms operating in complex black hole environments, and its capacity to differentiate between the effects of general relativity, the cosmological constant, and scalar, vector, and tensorial massive self-interacting field oscillations. This review concludes by examining the specific mathematical expressions characterizing the Weyl curvature index in the Newman-Penrose formalism, along with the key physical implications arising from these expressions. Code-mixed languages, which blend two or more languages within a single utterance, are ubiquitous in social media platforms and pose unique challenges for traditional language models. In multilingual communities, individuals often switch between multiple languages when communicating, even if they are fluent in each individual language. This code-mingling phenomenon holds particularly true on Twitter, where multiple languages are represented and spoken, yet standard language models struggle to accommodate these mixed expressions. This issue is particularly pronounced at the entity level, where names and labels often blend different languages, further complicating the problem. In essence, code-mingling requires models to simultaneously understand multiple languages, a skill that extends beyond simple language detection models. Code-mingling also introduces another challenge related to partial sharing of vocabulary, which can manifest as both intra- and inter-lingual word substitution. This research explores the intricate relationship between code-mingling, language switching, and vocabulary sharing, highlighting the distinct challenges each presents and the varied data sets available to address them. With an emphasis on real-world applications, this paper delves into the practical uses of code-mingling models within multilingual societies, also examining the promising integration of pre-trained models in these contexts. Ultimately, this work is poised to provide a comprehensive framework for further advancements in code-mingling model development and real-world implementation.

Quantifying the quality of automatic image descriptions is challenging due in part to their subjective nature. One commonly employed evaluation metric is the similarity between descriptions generated by a system and those included in the Image Folder of Referenceless Automatic Quality Evaluation. However, this approach relies on human-assigned quality scores for a small subset of images and does not account for the limited number of possible descriptions any given image can have. In fact, there are an estimated 10^42 distinct descriptions that could be generated for the Flickr set, far exceeding the number of descriptions provided by human annotators. As such, using the existing human-annotated descriptions to train a machine learning model does not significantly improve the efficacy of traditional metrics like BLEU or the recently introduced Description Understanding. Interestingly, our findings suggest that the current approach overestimates the diversity of descriptions, implying that real-world describers tend to use more similar descriptions than the data presently indicates. Ultimately, the prevalence of redundant descriptions also raises the risk of system bias towards describing images in ways that are analogous to how they have been described in the past. In an attempt to address these issues, we propose an alternative evaluation method based on the concept of description diversity and the Nash Equilibrium, which can be viewed as a proxy for measuring the closeness of generated descriptions to those provided by human annotators. This new approach is supported by experimental data showing its effectiveness in evaluating the quality of image description systems. The proposed method is also adaptable to other tasks that involve evaluating systems that generate diverse, naturally language-like outputs. The associated code is available for download at https://github.com/abhishek3915/Description-Diversity-Evaluation.

Our research involves a comprehensive examination of the Ta$_2$O$_5$ compound using first-principles calculations and Monte Carlo simulations for its ground-state lattice configuration. Ta$_2$O$_5$ exhibits polymorphism, and we investigated two forms: paraualum (alpha phase) and taalum (beta phase), examining their electronic structure, lattice parameters, and phonon spectra through simulation. Our results show that both phases have stable trajectories in the phase diagram, and we employed the Monte Carlo method to incorporate temperature effects. Ultimately, we determined that the energy difference between the two phases is very small, suggesting that temperature preferences might favor the beta phase over the alpha phase. However, to confidently conclude this, further experimental and theoretical analysis is required. Our derived beta phase results also demonstrate the compound's nonmetallic nature and lack of lattice anharmonicity. Lastly, we propose possible protocols for determining the beta phase's equilibrium lattice parameters at different temperatures. Ta$_2$O$_5$'s unique chemistry makes it challenging to model, but our approach provides a useful framework for tackling similar compounds with similar complexities. Lastly, we highlight the difficulties in achieving convergence for Ta$_2$O$_5$ using some screened hybrid DFT methods, and the implications of this for deriving the beta phase's electronic structure.

The Big Shift in geography during the COVID-19 pandemic had far-reaching consequences for physical and online interactions. We examined the effects of this shift on the spread of misinformation on Reddit. While the pandemic's peak saw increased online social connections, our findings suggest it also accelerated the dissemination of false information within Reddit's communities. The prolonged isolation during the winter months saw a significant shift in how false information was shared, with a detectable increase in misinformation spreading faster online. The Shift's impact on vaccination misinformation varied by location but generally correlated with low COVID-19 activity. The pandemic's peak saw a surge in conspiracy theories about the pandemic's origins, with variations tied to geographic location. The prevalence of false information decreased gradually after the winter months, with a notable decline in January 2021. The pandemic's end saw a decline in online social connections but no change in the speed at which false information was shared online. The Shift's impact on the circulation of misinformation was also reflected in the reduced online activity of Reddit users in low COVID-19 activity zones, with the slowest circulation of false information observed in the winter months. The The Big Shift's enduring impact on the circulation of misinformation is reflected in the continued spread of false information online, with the pandemic's legacy still felt in the low COVID-19 activity zones. The implications of these findings for public health policy and online misinformation mitigation strategies are discussed. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. When teaching robotic arms, demonstrating tasks visually is not sufficient as it does not account for possible misinterpretations of the arm's movements and the robot's motor constraints. Consequently, demonstrating tasks to robots requires a dual focus on both visual and auditory instruction. While the visual aspect illustrates the arm's movements and the objective of the task, the audio provides crucial information about the intended actions, helping the robot to better understand the underlying structure of the task. This visual-auditory teaching method is particularly beneficial when teaching novel tasks to robots. Our research involves examining which acoustic elements of demonstration instructions influence robotic learning and whether they affect the frequency and type of errors made during task execution. Our findings indicate that demonstration instructions containing a goal statement, a manipulation instruction, and an object label are all essential for reducing robotic errors. Furthermore, our data suggest that demonstrating tasks with a focus on the goal rather than the specific action taken to achieve it may lead to more frequent errors but with a different nature. This is crucial information for the development of spoken language-based robotic instruction frameworks that incorporate a goal-oriented approach. Ultimately, our research demonstrates a practical method for extracting pivotal acoustic information from demonstration instructions, a crucial step in developing such frameworks. This research received funding from AFOSR YIP Award, Google Cloud Research Award, Amazon Robotics Research Award, NSF Award, and the Bosch AI Lab. The data and models used in this research are available for download at https://yiyangli.github.io/project/teaching-with-sound/.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing system for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. This is an ongoing project, and we welcome collaborations that could help address these challenges and advance the testing infrastructure for conversational systems. This paper has been submitted to the AAAI-23 conference. The testing framework developed during this project is suited for real-world applications, as it can efficiently handle large-scale systems by only testing individual components, and supports cross-platorm compatibility. The framework, along with the authors' previous work, is now available on GitHub under the Apache-2 license. The testing framework has been utilized in real-world development scenarios, and has been found to significantly reduce testing costs by cutting the time spent on testing by up to 90%. The development of this framework has also sparked an ongoing discussion about the appropriate format for specifications in conversational system tests. The testing framework developed in this project is unique in that it uses a simple, intuitive text-based format for specifications, and has been compared to a more complex, graph-based format that it was found to be equivalent to. The development of this framework has also led to an ongoing exploration of the challenge of comparing the meaning of utterances in conversational systems, and an initial approach has been outlined in the paper. Cross-domain recommendation has gained significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single or dual sparse domains are not representative or common in real-world scenarios, making dual sparse domains the least considered case. Most existing methods focus on combining features or exchanging knowledge between domains, which may compromise the effectiveness in dense domains due to information contamination. Furthermore, the category-based preference learning framework, which is effective in managing complex preference information, has been underutilized in cross-domain recommendation. In this paper, a novel method called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation via Category-Based Preference Learning is proposed to address these limitations. It incorporates a novel category-based preference learning framework to manage complex preference information and develops a dual-domain strategy and a parameter-free selective cross-domain transfer approach to address data sparsity in multiple domains and information contamination. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method. The proposed method is applicable to multiple-domain scenarios, not limited to dual sparse domains. The method can be extended to tackle other challenging scenarios, such as multi-attribute recommendation and recommendation with multiple sparse attributes. The code of the proposed method is available at https://github.com/zhengyang98/MSDCR.

Conic equations are a fundamental building block in optimization, allowing the incorporation of various constraints such as semidefinite, non-negative matrix, and Euclidean matrix constraints. We introduce Hypatia, a Julia library that generates convex optimization problems from scratch, utilizing a wide range of conic equations, including newly proposed natural conic equations and their relationships. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in solving large-scale problems, specifically tackling self-duality equations that underlie various semidefinite programming applications. Furthermore, we exhibit the versatility of our method in incorporating multiple conic equations within a single optimization problem, and in defining the objective function from an arbitrary natural conic equation. With Hypatia, we also investigate a novel non-rigid body rotation cone that leads to a self-duality equation, and demonstrate the presence of this new cone within an existing one, thereby implying its potential utility in specific semidefinite programming contexts. The Hypatia library is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/parthean/Hypatia.jl.

The escalating number of MRI scans necessitates efficient quality control, making automated image assessment crucial. This assessment can be further simplified by identifying which MRI scans require no additional quality assurance beyond their assigned label. Our approach addresses this challenge by incorporating a multi-factorial generalization framework, incorporating multiple factors such as imaging protocols, anatomical regions, and abnormality diagnoses in MRI scans. This approach allows for the prediction of image assessment labels and differentiates between scans that require no further assessment beyond their already assigned label. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach, with results showing that considering multiple factors, particularly imaging protocols and anatomical regions, is crucial for accurate image assessment. This is particularly evident when analyzing scans with normal anatomy, as they are accurately assessed even with the inclusion of irrelevant factors. On the other hand, scans with lesions are more challenging to assess, as they are often incorrectly classified when unnecessary factors are included. This finding underlines the complexity of this task and the need for large datasets that account for real-world imaging practices. This challenge is particularly pronounced when analyzing scans with different protocol variations, as this is a true multi-factorial generalization problem. This is also reflected in the high error rates observed with common deep learning techniques that overfit to specific protocols and protocols variations. This research highlights the importance of sufficient protocol change tolerance in models to prevent overfitting and ensure that models are capable of handling novel combinations of protocols and variations that they have never seen before. This is a critical issue that affects not only image assessment but also other applications that involve models with high tolerance for novel data combinations. This is further demonstrated by the fact that models that are capable of handling novel combinations of protocols and variations, even with additional factors such as anatomical regions and abnormality diagnoses in MRI scans, are more likely to accurately assess scans that require no further assessment beyond their already assigned label. To prevent power grid disruptions and ensure the stability of distribution systems, overproduction during peak energy periods is often necessary. However, this approach results in excessive energy generation costs and environmental impacts during off-peak periods with sufficient energy supply. This paper proposes a novel multi-agent optimization framework that minimizes the costs of peak and off-peak energy production by incorporating plug-in electric vehicles (EVs) as energy storage devices. In this scheme, a decentralized optimization algorithm is developed to determine optimal charging/discharging schedules for individual EVs, while a higher-level decision maker determines optimal charging/discharging orders for individual EVs to ensure the stability of the distribution system. The proposed framework considers various EV behaviors, including private ownership, and evaluates its effectiveness in a real-world test case. The results show that this approach reduces production costs and environmental impacts while preventing grid disruptions. The proposed method can be applied to various energy management scenarios with EVs. The optimization algorithm developed in this research can also be adapted for use in other applications involving decentralized optimization with shared variables. In the realm of computer-generated meetings, characters' engaging conversations are facilitated by a combination of dialogue and physical movement within virtual meeting spaces. This approach requires an integrated approach that involves multiple systems, including dialogue production, spatial control, and motivation to drive character behavior. To efficiently develop this kind of integrated system, we've introduced a new approach based on independent, fully functional modules that can be easily combined. This approach allows developers to experiment with different dialogue generation techniques, various spatial control methods, and multiple motivation systems to create diverse character behaviors. We've put this approach to use in creating a simple dialogue system and demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in an online demonstration. This approach is suitable for use in public settings and can be applied to various types of meetings. The underlying code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghasemzade/.

Recently, our group examined the crystal, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3 and CmSn3 from first principles, using the GPA and PAW methods with full relativistic effects. Our study indicated that CmSn3 possesses a trigonal distortion of the TiNi3 structure with the DoS type of magnetic behavior, whereas GdSn3 has a tetragonal structure with the semi-metallic DoS characteristics. By constructing the (100) (110) (001) sequence of superlattices, we also explored the electronic and magnetic properties of the GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds with x = 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, and 1. The results for x = 1/2 and 3/4 showed the TiNi3 and AuCu3 structures with the semi-metallic and DoS type of magnetic behavior respectively, whereas x = 2/3 and 1 featured the TiNi3 and AuCu3 structures with the semi-metallic and DoS type of magnetic behavior respectively. The most suitable x value for the TiNi3 and AuCu3 structures with the semi-metallic and DoS type of magnetic behavior respectively was found to be 1; this structure had been previously unknown. The program FBAM (Forecasts of Additional Baryons and Mesons) predicts the existence of missing enteries in the particle spectrum. Based on a comprehensive review of existing data, FBAM anticipates findings of new mesons and baryons, shedding light on quark combinations and potentially revealing signs of exotic matter. A highlight of the program is the particle database it maintains, covering over 300 observed particles and 1000 predicted ones. FBAM further provides statistical models incorporating mass and charge patterns, and it offers predictions for future experimental discoveries at various energy levels. The program is adaptable to be used with data from past and ongoing experiments, such as ALICE, CMS, LHCb, and others, as well as with forecasts for upcoming facilities like the EIC, GLUE, MESA, and the LHC's upcoming upgrades. The predictions and methodologies employed by FBAM are intended to facilitate collaboration with physicists and provide a starting point for further analysis based on actual data findings. The program is openly accessible at https://fbam.hep.anl.gov/.

Utilizing Pantheon SN Ia data and combining it with a weak lensing map, we identified a significant correlation between the average weak lensing distortion and the intrinsic brightness of supernovae. This correlation's magnitude is precisely 0.38 magnitudes and is highly significant, surpassing 4 sigma. By accounting for various influences, we determined the primary cause of the observed trend to be cosmic-scale structure rather than the effects of the Milky Way or the supernovae's own intrinsic variability. The scale of this structure was estimated at 10-20 $h^{-1}$ Mpc, and we calculated the current weak lensing standard deviation on the supernovae's intrinsic brightness to be 0.055 magnitudes. Furthermore, we explored the potential for similar effects in other SN Ia datasets and found the current data to be insufficient for drawing definite conclusions about similar lensing influences in other datasets. Lastly, we discussed the implications of these findings for the justice metric and the justice factor, along with the possible uses of the average lensing distortion as a variable in SN Ia analyses. Our proposed evaluation metric, ContextScore, assesses object detection models' ability to incorporate context effectively. This metric compares the predictions made by a model with a full-field of view to those made by a model with a restricted field of view, specifically one that is blinded to a section of the image. Our research indicates that ContextScore correlates strongly with the benefits gained from using a larger field of view, which is a key indicator of a model's ability to utilize context. By examining the relationship between ContextScore and various deep learning object detection architectures and training protocols, we identified areas for improvement in the design of these methods. Our findings suggest that a model's capacity to utilize context is a distinct aspect that can be contrasted with its ability to recognize patterns, and thus it should be treated as a separate performance metric in its own right. We further discovered that the difference in performance between a model with a full-field of view and one with a blinded field of view varies significantly over the course of an object detection task's training process. By analyzing the context's impact on state-of-the-art object detection models at various levels of complexity, we identified a crucial limitation in the design of the current deep learning object detection architectures, specifically with regard to their ability to utilize context. We demonstrated the efficacy of this design by implementing a simple and efficient residual learning method, which significantly improved the performance of a model with a blinded field of view to a degree that is comparable to a model with a full-field of view. When allocating organs, a compatible match isn't always found between willing recipients and available donors. This study examines the strategic approach transplant candidates should take when encountering such a situation, specifically when it comes to accepting kidneys from unrelated donors. It's assumed that candidates can selectively choose to participate in the organ allocation process and that donors are willing to donate to any compatible candidate. The study goes on to analyze a key scenario where the number of compatible matches between recipients and donors exceeds the number of available kidney transplants. It finds that, in this case, the optimal strategy for candidates to follow involves participating in the process, as it leads to more successful transplants and greater overall satisfaction. It's also discovered that, under certain conditions, accepting any incompatible transplant won't be part of the optimal strategy. The study also explores what happens when candidates can choose between different organ allocation processes and finds that, in some cases, the optimal approach involves creating artificial waiting lists to increase transparency and honesty among candidates and, as a result, reduces dishonest behavior to some extent. A dynamic network model is proposed, where two individuals engage in a random encounter, and based on their infected status, they connect in one of two ways. If one person is infected and the other isn't, their connection strengthens, whereas a random node in the network is targeted for a new connection during uninfected encounters. This model incorporates elements of both preferential attachment and assortative mixing. By analyzing the model's parameters, it becomes apparent that this dynamic network exhibits a balance between a fully connected state and a more complex, richer structure. By simulating uncorrelated random walks within this dynamic network, it was found that they converge more quickly than they do in a static, fully random model. This is especially true for larger networks and certain walk starting conditions. This model and its variants have been shown to replicate the spread of infectious diseases as well as uncorrelated random walks within a given population. This leads to an interesting dilemma where the mechanism that generates the network also facilitates the disease spread, creating an obstacle to its own effectiveness. This issue is at the heart of two proposed epidemic prevention strategies: one that targets individual connections and another that aims to eliminate small groups of connected individuals. This approach is particularly effective in stopping the spread of diseases that affect multiple groups. This research also explores the relationship between random walks and disease spread within a network that changes over time and finds that both converge more quickly in larger networks. This finding is especially true for networks with multiple distinct groups and can be attributed to the network's dynamic nature, which promotes greater exploration and faster convergence. This is a key finding because it highlights the benefits of networks that change over time and provide better protection against both external invasion and the spread of diseases. This research into dynamic networks that change over time also provides a framework for exploring and analyzing the parameters that govern them. This framework is particularly useful for uncovering the underlying patterns and dynamics of networks that arise from random encounters between individuals in a population. This research into preventive rewiring networks that change over time has been a focused area of study within the broader field of evolutionary games, dynamic networks, and epidemiology. Our proposed technique as well as its related methods are efficient, requiring minimal computational resources and memory to operate. This modification aims to address general relativity's shortcomings, specifically its incompatibility with the energy positivity requirement and the absence of a well-defined nonlocal gravity operator in certain contexts. Based on this approach, we derive nonlocal gravity equations that describe how the modified stress-energy tensor evolves over time in response to the gravitational field. These equations take the form of integro-differential equations that can be analyzed to understand how the nonlocal effects change with time and distance. Next, we simplify these equations to better understand their fundamental characteristics. Finally, we discuss the implications of these equations for the gravitational field's behavior in both empty and matter-filled spacetimes. In the process, we encounter the nonlocal gravity potential, a new fundamental concept that serves as a direct analogue to the general relativity potential. However, unlike the general relativity potential, the nonlocal gravity potential cannot be expressed in terms of the nonlocal stress-energy tensor's divergence. Rather, it is found to be related to the nonlocal stress-energy tensor's curl, a distinction with significant physical implications. This capability can be leveraged to perform three distinct functions. Firstly, to enhance the understanding of single nuclei-proton interactions by analyzing the isobar scattering data off protons at the LHC. Secondly, to perform precise measurements of certain rare processes in the weak interaction sector, similar to neutrino scattering, on protons or lead nuclei. Thirdly, to investigate the possibility of performing deuteron-gold or heavy-heavy collisions at the LHC's full design energy. Utilizing the LHC's extensive detector suite, renowned for its high-precision and comprehensive particle measurement capabilities, offers a strong potential for obtaining rich and accurate data from these minor systems. Consequently, the potential for delivering substantial scientific gains from the LHC's capability to produce small systems at RHIC-like intensities is evident. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A key argument for this claim is based on the behavior of extragalactic neutron star binary systems, specifically how often their X-ray binaries repeat. For the Andromeda Galaxy's NRX J205803.47409529+463829.840143 and M31 NRX J053431.67703594-675454.570034, researchers found the recurrence periods of their X-ray binaries to be quite long - over 10 to 20 years. This statistic is used to counter the black hole hypothesis for the Milky Way's quiescent X-ray binaries, suggesting that the lack of outbursts in the Galacitic Centre's X-ray binaries may be due to detection limitations rather than an absence of active binaries. The paper also examines the distribution of recurrence intervals for a larger sample of neutron star binary systems, specifically those associated with the Galactic Centre, the Andromeda Galaxy, and the Large Magellanic Cloud, with the aim of distinguishing between different distribution patterns that could reflect the binaries' nature or the outburst detection bias. The paper's findings suggest that the distribution of recurrence intervals in the Andromeda Galaxy and the Large Magellanic Cloud align with the extrapolated long-period distribution of the Galactic Centre, with the exception of one notable LMC system with a short recurrence period. The paper's analysis indicates that the lack of outbursts in the Galacitic Centre's X-ray binaries may indeed be attributed to the binaries' nature rather than the lack of active binaries, with approximately half of the Galacitic Centre's X-ray binaries being expected to display an outburst within the next 10 to 20 years. The paper's findings also provide an estimate for the outburst recurrence period of the Milky Way's X-ray binary GRS 1757-424 to be around 10 to 20 years. The paper's results further support the hypothesis that the variable X-ray source 4U 1850-06 is a neutron star binary rather than a black hole binary. Additionally, analogies with living organisms where sound and heat waves interact with cells and proteins may also be drawn from this research. Lastly, this study highlights the significance of incorporating time-dependent variables in the analysis of strained and magnetic solids.

When engaging in conversations, people often employ different types of reasoning, which can be categorized into various semantic varieties. In this study, we introduce a novel framework, NLI Dialogue with Variety (NDV), which incorporates multiple semantic varieties and presents a series of dialogue choices to users, each related to a specific variety. The chosen dialogues are then scored based on their connection to a particular variety, making it possible to measure the semantic variety exhibited in conversations. NDV includes a companion training task to enhance the quality of the dialogues and reduces the problem to a more manageable assessment of conversation diversity. We also design an alternative version, NDV-Choice, which allows a single NLI choice to be made from four varied options. Both NDV and NDV-Choice are evaluated using human raters, and the results demonstrate a connection between the dialogue varieties and ratings obtained. Furthermore, NDV-Choice is compared to existing NLI choice evaluation methods. The introduction of NDV provides a meaningful framework for exploring conversation diversity, and future research opportunities in this area are discussed. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, but are often hindered by the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. We mitigate this challenge by introducing a data-dependent kernel feature map, incorporating a deterministic shift that significantly reduces the required number of random Fourier features while achieving comparable performance. We derive optimal shift values to minimize dimensionality without compromising accuracy, and demonstrate the benefits of our approach in high-dimensional pairwise evaluations, particularly in deep learning models and with limited training data. The resulting method surpasses random Fourier features in multiple benchmarks, even when employing substantially fewer features. Moreover, we find it to be highly efficient in estimating the Gram matrix, accurately enough to serve as a substitute in several applications. The method is available as the Python package 'ddkfe' on PyPI.

Network systems are frequently prone to catastrophic failures and we examine the breakdown of a specific type of network, composed of non-neighbor link connections, using the independent destruction model. As the networks destroy themselves, we identify the locations where removals are most likely to occur and determine that areas connected to the system's perimeter have a higher chance of being damaged. Ultimately, we determine the conditions under which the network collapses suddenly or gradually. Additionally, we establish that eliminating the outerly connected nodes first leads to the system's gradual collapse, whereas removing the centrally connected nodes first leads to the system's rapid collapse. Furthermore, we find that the shift from the gradual to the rapid collapse scenario is marked by an increase in the average shortest path length from 2 to 4 as the network's central area becomes increasingly disconnected. Lastly, we compare our findings to those of a previous study on a different destruction model.

This research focuses on creating precise, long-lasting Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions, taking advantage of multiple vibrational modes to enhance efficiency and minimize duration. By matching multiple mode amplitudes and optimizing gate duration, a balanced combination of motion modes is found to significantly reduce frequency fluctuations and duration-related errors. By adjusting mode contributions, a frequency stability of one percent can be achieved within a time frame that is roughly ten times shorter than optimally configured single-mode gates. Furthermore, modulating the ground state motional modes' initial conditions allows for improved frequency stability and reduces the required beam strength, but it also increases the necessary duration. In addition, using two cross-talk-free motion modes yields identical results, indicating that this approach is compatible with multiple beam configurations. Lastly, this frequency-stable gate implementation is compatible with subsequent, precise quantum operations, and it meets the requirements for generating non-classical states and implementing quantum error correction protocols. We propose a multi-orbital honeycomb lattice model featuring a precise replica of the Dirac fermion spectrum seen in graphene, yet with highly correlated electrons. By adjusting an external electric field, the spatial symmetry of the model can be altered from hexagonal to rectangular symmetry. This change in symmetry allows us to explore the interplay of geometric frustration and anisotropic Dirac dispersion in a single model. Our predictions include the presence of three distinct phases in the rectangular geometry: a strong ferromagnetic phase, a uniform phase, and a phase with stripes. The predicted phase diagrams can be tested using experimental and theoretical means, offering a precise replica of graphene's Dirac fermion spectrum with electronic correlations. A suitable material, Li-intercalated Pd(111), is also identified as a potential realization of this model.

Researchers explored the NA62 experiment's capacity to detect heavy neutral leptons at the Kaon decay process, analyzing the reaction $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$. By considering various heavy neutral lepton masses, they evaluated observable effects and established thresholds for different decay modes. Combining existing data with optimized production cuts for heavy neutral lepton masses within the 0.01 to 100 GeV range, the team calculated detection probabilities for heavy neutral lepton masses below 0.25 GeV through the observation of missing energy in the electron or neutral kaon channels. In the 0.25 to 100 GeV range, they focused on detecting electrons in the neutral kaon channel. Estimating detection efficiencies at the NA62 production site, the team calculated expected detection rates for heavy neutral leptons at various masses and compared this with existing data from the CERN PS and the LHCb experiment. Combining these results with solid production cross-section data, they calculated the heavy neutral lepton production cross-section at the NA62 production site for different masses. Finally, the team calculated the number of heavy neutral lepton events that could be detected at the NA62 experiment within a certain data collection period and compared this with existing data from the NA62 experiment, concluding that they could detect heavy neutral leptons with masses between $4.5 \times 10^{-3}$ and $2.3$ GeV with certain coupling values. The team also identified the most sensitive channel to heavy neutral lepton detection and proposed several optimization strategies to enhance detection capabilities. The predicted results were validated through realistic simulation studies. The research demonstrated the NA62 experiment's capacity to detect heavy neutral leptons across a broad mass range with certain coupling values and suggested several optimization strategies to further improve detection capabilities. The findings were relevant to other heavy neutral lepton production processes at the NA62 experiment. The research outcomes were a theoretical expression for heavy neutral lepton effects on Kaon decay processes and estimated detection probabilities for heavy neutral leptons at the NA62 experiment. The results were derived from theoretical analysis and validated through realistic simulation studies. Neural text generation models have surpassed traditional $N$-gram models in performance but are impractical for real-time applications due to their large size. This research explores the possibility of combining neural networks with $N$-gram models for more efficient text creation. A novel training method is introduced that employs a neural network as a prior and learns a neural network in a residual manner using $N$-gram models as an initial guess. The resulting model achieves comparable results to neural networks in the low-vocabulary scenario and significantly outperforms them in the high-vocabulary scenario, with a marked reduction in size. The models also exhibit improved performance in pseudocode generation tasks. The code for this research has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/res-ngram.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial data. This research introduces an innovative end-to-end technique called SADRNet, which produces a highly durable 3D face reconstruction model, namely a Triangular Mesh, by employing a dual-face regression framework and a self-alignment process. A key aspect of this method is a face partition technique that divides the model into distinct regions, reducing the negative impact of facial occlusions. A robust regression component then employs two separate face models to derive a unified, occlusion-resistant reconstruction by minimizing the discrepancy between them. A self-alignment process among points derived from the face regions ensures a cohesive, detailed reconstruction. Evaluations using the widely accepted FaceWarehouse database demonstrate the superiority of our approach, and an assessment using a publicly accessible 3D face reconstruction platform also ranks our method highly. Moreover, an analysis of real-world images shows that our technique can effectively handle facial occlusions in natural images. The code for this research has been made publicly accessible on GitHub.

In $\alpha$-attractor inflation models, a specific type of perturbation with an exact solution can cause problems when the inflationary regime shifts, potentially resulting in an excessive scalar field roll. This excessive roll might exceed the field's stability threshold, leading to the formation of oscillons or cosmological solitons and ultimately their collapse into primordial black holes. We calculate the scalar field roll and determine its relationship with the inflationary parameters, and compare it to the threshold for oscillon formation. This comparison allows us to identify a boundary beyond which oscillon or soliton formation is inevitable, and also to determine the associated mass fraction of primordial black holes. This black hole fraction decreases with increasing peak roll amplitude, but also depends on the specific $\alpha$-attractor model used. We analyze three distinct models from the literature with different roll thresholds due to their differing inflationary dynamics. This discrepancy highlights the importance of using models that match the observed roll amplitude rather than overestimating based on scaling laws. This is particularly relevant as the roll amplitude affects the formation of oscillatons rather than solitons, with oscillatons forming when the roll is below a certain peak amplitude, while solitons form when the roll exceeds this threshold. This distinction leads to distinct black hole mass fractions for each model type. This research also explains the roll amplitude's effect on the formed black hole mass fraction, showing that it is a consequence of the oscillaton/soliton formation rather than a direct result of the cosmological perturbations. This indicates that the primary contribution to the PBH mass fraction comes from a narrow range of the roll amplitude distribution rather than a broad one, with the exact fraction depending on specific model characteristics. This finding is a critical insight into the relationship between the roll amplitude and black hole mass fractions, and it has implications for models used to explain the observed PBH population, suggesting that a broader range of models, including those with different roll amplitude distributions, should be examined in the future. This includes models with log-normal roll amplitude distributions, which could potentially fit the observed PBH mass fraction spectrum by shifting the peak roll amplitude distribution. This could also explain the presence of PBHs with lower masses, which are difficult to explain through the oscillaton/soliton collapse of the standard $\alpha$-attractor model used in the future, as they would have arisen in a different future era. With an eye on applying mathematical concepts to these linguistic models, we delve into studying the highest leaf nodes of marked ordered trees, which we call "deepest vertices." In this study, we establish the probability distribution of the deepest vertices occurring at a particular level $h$ in binary marked ordered trees. To derive this distribution, we use the combinatorial approach of counting the number of binary marked ordered trees by examining the arrangements of left-branching subtrees and using the formula for the Catalan numbers. We then determine the expected value of the deepest vertex level, which serves as an analog to the well-known result for unmarked binary trees. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the deepest vertex level and the number of nodes in the tree, which enables us to determine the probability distribution of the deepest vertex level for non-binary marked ordered trees. This phenomenon has been explained by two distinct mechanisms: one related to the spectrum of the data matrix and the other to the distribution of the data itself. Building on this work, we explore over-parametrized linear models in dynamic time series scenarios and discover that they too can cope with model mismatches while achieving low test errors. Here, the focus is on a single-time series scenario with stationary data. We establish non-asymptotic bounds for the benign overfitting scenario, extending the results from static data to dynamic scenarios with a focus on the spectrum of the data matrix. Furthermore, we investigate the validity of these bounds in asymptotic regimes characteristic of large datasets. The asymptotic analysis also facilitates an understanding of the interplay between the sample size, dataset dimensionality, and data timeframe on the dynamics of model performance. A key issue in the development of a decentralized energy system is an efficient management of storage devices. In a model with multiple markets, we examine optimized storage usage across various sectors, including supply, demand, and a trading platform, while accounting for information asymmetry. A novel self-allocation mechanism, based on a range of valuation probabilities, is developed to ensure that each storage unit is utilized by an informed or a retail market participant. This mechanism is proven to satisfy three key properties: validity, individual rationality, and efficiency. Additionally, it is demonstrated that this mechanism is risk-neutral in regards to valuation, making it an equitable solution for participants of varying risk appetites. A numerical example is provided to illustrate the practical application of this mechanism. A comparative analysis with existing solutions highlights the benefits of this self-allocation mechanism in a real-world context. A storage allocation model with consideration for risk is also introduced, offering an alternative solution to this problem. This model is validated through numerical testing and compares favorably to the self-allocation mechanism. A notable difference is seen when storage devices with distinct characteristics are utilized. In such cases, the risk-aware model is capable of accurately valuing these assets, while the risk-neutral mechanism overvalues them due to their limited availability. This leads to an influx of these devices in the retail market and potentially inadequate access to them in other sectors. This issue could be mitigated by implementing a commission-based storage allocation fee in the retail market. A numerical analysis of this solution is also presented. A risk-aware storage allocation model with consideration for information asymmetry is a more complex problem that remains unsolved at the time of this writing. A model with exogenous prices is developed as a starting point towards addressing this issue. It is demonstrated that this model is valid, individually rational, and efficient, but it does not offer any additional benefits over a risk-neutral solution when prices are known with certainty. When there is uncertainty associated with prices, this model offers a risk-aware solution and is capable of handling distributional valuation. A numerical analysis of this solution is also presented. A risk-aware storage allocation model with endogenous prices that accounts for information asymmetry and distributional valuation is a problem that remains unsolved at the time of this writing. A possible solution to this problem could be found by applying the concepts of robust mechanism design. A numerical analysis is presented for a model with uncertainty associated with prices and a valuation range, offering a risk-aware solution and a comparative analysis with existing solutions. A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Similar patterns emerge when this space is projected in different dimensionless forms, allowing previous and current research on this subject to be compared. Furthermore, our models simulate circulation styles previously thought to be exclusive to larger planet simulations, such as super-rotation in low-oblateness and rapid rotation scenarios, as well as cyclostrophic turbulence in intermediate rotation rates, aligning with theoretical expectations. Additionally, we find that the transition from super-rotation to turbulence speeds up with increasing external heat sources, while the transition from turbulence to cyclostrophic balance slows down. Conversely, it slows down with faster planet rotation in the intermediate rotation regime, but speeds up in the fast rotation regime. Finally, by directly observing the initial breakdown of solid body rotation, our models also identify an previously unreported stage of turbulence called "turbulent annulus", bounded by two circular rings where atmospheric motion moves in opposite directions. This marks the first known instance of which a state of atmospheric turbulence occurs on a rotating planet.

Our key innovation involves creating a trainable module that identifies peer models requiring similar data and learns from their own effectiveness, thereby producing a more efficient collaborative learning model. By transitioning to an end-to-end trainability setting, we find that the model can determine optimal peer models and even determine the optimal set of models to collaborate with. In turn, this leads to a model that optimally selects models to collaborate with, thus achieving a true dynamic learning model. When applied to real-world tasks, this model achieves collaborative learning results comparable to those obtained through meticulous dataset and peer model selection processes. Moreover, by transitioning to an end-to-end trainability setting, we are able to leverage the vast amount of data available for ImageNet, thereby setting a new record for classification accuracy on this scale. Specifically, our model achieves a 89.05% top-1 classification accuracy on ImageNet, thus surpassing previous collaborative learning-based records and achieving the highest accuracy to date on this benchmark. The code for our model is publicly available at https://github.com/DeepMind/Dynamic-Learning.

To advance further, demonstrating the ability to execute reliable two-qubit logic operations with a strong coupling between qubits and facilitating the execution of the necessary exchange-coupled operations between them, precise simulation of exchange-coupled donors is necessary. This study involves computationally modeling two donors that are coupled through exchange interaction within the silicon multi-valley effective mass theory, and it provides a comprehensive understanding of how electron interaction, location-based mass variation, and valley mixing effects influence the donors' behavior, particularly on their ability to execute reliable two-qubit logic operations. Variations in valley mixing are found to affect the coupling strength significantly, with certain configurations actually increasing the coupling, contrary to the generally held belief that larger valley mixing leads to weaker coupling. Additionally, this research identifies the most desirable mass and charge distribution configurations for efficient two-qubit operations. In the course of this study, we also develop a method for efficiently simulating the behavior of multiple-valley electrons by employing a combination of configuration interaction and a simplified multi-valley effective mass theory. In the process, we extracted the necessary electronic wave functions from the lattice space, and these findings are applicable to [111] and [100] oriented silicon interfaces. The developed simulation method is capable of handling up to 10-valley configurations and can incorporate variations in valley mixing, mass, and charge distribution with ease. Our investigation employs a scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy approach to explore the quantum conduction of individual HgTe quantum wells at their critical thickness. Real-time measurements of differential tunneling currents through potential barriers within the wells reveal the spatial dependence of their conductance. As expected, within the range of large positive and negative thickness disparities from the critical point, conductance correlates with the energy of the Dirac electrons residing within the wells' energy bands. However, at and very close to the critical thickness, the conductance displays unique, unprecedented behavior tied to the electrons' energy and indicative of the spatial extent of the electron's "tail" beyond the point of charge confinement. By combining our findings with theoretical models, we gain insights into this conductance's origin and the precise mechanisms governing electron confinement in HgTe quantum wells. Additionally, our discovery paves the way for utilizing low-dimensional Dirac materials in tunneling devices and others that rely on precise, controlled electron confinement.

In order to increase bandwidth efficiency, cellular networks employ dynamic Time Division Duplexing (TDD), where different models schedule uplink and downlink time slots. However, this feature introduces conflicts when combining TDD models from different base stations. This research focuses on optimizing resource allocation across TDD models in cellular networks using advanced Self-Organizing Network capabilities. Initially, a mathematical framework is presented to facilitate efficient scheduling. Next, a precise algorithm is developed to calculate optimal solutions for small-scale networks. Finally, an efficient, simple approach is devised to achieve near-optimal solutions in larger, more complex networks. Both algorithms are put to the test in a simulated environment mirroring real-world conditions. The evaluation reveals that the simple approach offers a suitable compromise between efficiency and optimal performance in practical scenarios. The research ultimately presents a framework for managing TDD models in small and large cellular networks, making it a valuable contribution to the field. The findings also support utilizing the default TDD configuration specified in LTE standards. In this study, a novel neural network model called HDN is presented, which is capable of generating derivatives as its output. Based on Hamiltonian dynamics, this model incorporates differential equations as input and employs a straightforward feed-forward architecture to train its components. A significant advantage of HDN is that it avoids the requirement for inverse differential techniques, which are known to be challenging, especially when attempting to train deep networks. Our investigation into HDN demonstrates that it is capable of accurately replicating derivatives, including those obtained through numerical differentiation, by generating overfits of data provided. Additionally, as a practical application, HDN is used to create a simple model for estimating time-series derivatives, which in turn is utilized to improve the performance of LSTMs in the task of stock price prediction. Our findings are supported by comprehensive experimental results, which demonstrate the superiority of HDN over competing methods. As a notable exception, when attempting to learn the derivative of a sine function, our model fails to converge, although this is shown to be an insoluble problem even for numerical methods. As HDN places derivatives on an equal footing with inputs, it offers a new perspective on the concept of "input/derivative" symmetry present in Hamiltonian dynamics. This in turn is reflected in a proposed modification to the Hamiltonian dynamics framework, which we term "extended Hamiltonian dynamics" or EHD. This EHD includes hidden variables on an equal footing with inputs and positions, and includes both input and position as conserved quantities within a specific Hamiltonian dynamics setting. This new perspective on Hamiltonian dynamics is demonstrated to be effective in modeling real-world phenomena, specifically in the prediction of stock prices. This model is distinct from conventional Hamiltonian dynamics-based neural networks, and represents an innovative direction for future research. This approach allows models to learn from each other and correct mistakes, thereby improving their accuracy. A simulation of a self-driving scenario and real-world medical diagnostics data demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. The findings indicate that our approach not only boosts the models' performance but also adapts to changing environments with ease. The primary goal of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) is to accurately determine the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Despite significant progress in Natural Language Processing, WSD remains a challenging task even for the current state-of-the-art models.  In this research, we concentrate on the fundamental issue of word sense disambiguation and present a novel approach, Context-gloss Enhancement for WSD.  This approach commences by creating a glossary of sorts, which includes context snippets paired with the corresponding word senses.  These pairs are then used to train a context-gloss model that enhances the relevant glosses to direct the model towards a particular word sense.  We leverage a previously developed framework to train the context-gloss model, thereby obtaining a set of latent vectors that effectively capture the essence of the target word senses.  To achieve the desired outcome, we simply add these vectors to the input of the pre-trained model, which significantly boosts the performance of word sense disambiguation.  Our results indicate that this simple approach, when employed within the BERT-based framework, surpasses the current state-of-the-art outcomes in three widely recognized WSD evaluation datasets.  Moreover, when used within the strong Multilingual Masked Language Modeling alone, it delivers comparable performance to the existing records.  The code for this project is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Context-gloss-Enhancement-for-WSD.

This study develops a series of intensified integral definitions for the reciprocal Gamma function, extending the basic Riemann, trapezoidal, and compound trapezoidal formulas, as well as a modified trapezoidal formula and a Boisobas formula, by incorporating regularization techniques. The intensified formulas, with lower error terms than their unregularized counterparts, incorporate coefficients derived from Eulerian gamma functions or other means, providing equivalent accuracy to the unregularized versions. A comparison with the unregularized compound trapezoidal formula shows that the regularized version exhibits a quadratically greater convergence rate. Additionally, the study establishes the relationship between the intensified formulas and the unregularized compound trapezoidal formula, enabling the computation of the Eulerian gamma function via numerical integration. A further analysis of the intensified formulas' convergence rates, with respect to both step size and the number of subintervals, is presented. We introduce a new efficient method for resolving the most probable explanation (MPE) and constrained optimisation problems in graphical models, ourftw. This approach differs from existing techniques by eschewing the use of belief propagation. Instead, our method directly manipulates the functional representation of our model, known as its "brief function representation" (BFR). We demonstrate in ourftw how the BFR can be derived from a model's normalised exponential family representation, and showcase the simplicity of its structure. Our results show that solving for the BFR is computationally efficient and can be done in O(n) time, where n is the number of variables in the model. Furthermore, this representation enables us to solve MPE and constrained optimisation problems in linear time, and to efficiently determine tree decomposition boundaries in O(n) time. We also explore how ourftw can be combined with existing methods, such as branch and cut, to solve complex, large-scale problems. We validate ourftw on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, and compare its performance favourably to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Our code is available online at https://github.com/ourftw/ourftw.

Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. As a result, the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$ is determined as well as the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. Additionally, an invariant theoretic approach is used to establish a sequence of algebras known as the universal enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, and the polynomial algebra $\mathbb{C}[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ all share a Hilbert-Poincar\'e sequence.

Google Web search uses personalisation to tailor results for individual users based on their search history and account settings. This study examines the impact of such personalisation on the discovery of relevant information on the web. A controlled experiment was conducted in which the same set of 39 openly available online articles were made searchable for two groups of Google users through different search interfaces. The interfaces were designed to deliver the same search algorithm used in standard Google Web search, with the exception of displaying up to 10 search results per page. The first group consisted of 400 random Google users, while the second group comprised 400 users whose accounts were linked to Google and had a Google Account, but with no search history. The task given to the users in both groups was to find any relevant information among the searchable articles. The results showed that users with Google Accounts found fewer relevant articles (22 out of 39) compared to random Google users (34 out of 39). Furthermore, a separate analysis of user navigation within the interface revealed that users with Google Accounts were more likely to click on the same small set of highly ranked search results, missing up to 60% of the available relevant information. The study highlights the potential drawbacks of web search personalisation, including the possibility that users with Google Accounts may overlook a substantial quantity of relevant information. The findings have implications for both individuals and institutions that rely on Google Web search for knowledge discovery. A novel approach to tracking and accounting for respiratory movement in magnetic resonance imaging has been developed to ensure highly accurate and motion-reduced images in inhalation-exhalation T2-weighted imaging. Utilizing real-time monitoring of respiratory patterns, the technique involves modulating the data collection phase to align it with the exhalation phase of each respiratory cycle. Following data acquisition, the algorithm performs a correction for residual motion and artifacts. The results showed that this method outperformed conventional techniques in terms of motion reduction, artifact diminishment, and patient comfort, with over 90% of the images being motion-free and suitable for clinical use. This technique has been successfully applied in abdominal imaging with excellent results. The technique's open design also allows it to be combined with other motion-reducing strategies with excellent results.
