A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping volumes, new ship prices, used ship prices, and scrapped ship values has been assembled from 1966 to 2009 for the five main shipping routes. Approximately 1,500 observations are available for each of the five routes, with the exception of route 3, which has 1,200 observations. A previous study using a subset of route 3 data found that freight rates, initially caused to fluctuate randomly, were actually driven by shipping volumes. The newly expanded dataset allows for freight rate and shipping volume dynamics to be reexamined across all five routes. The data compilation methodology is outlined in detail, along with the freight rate and shipping volume models used for analysis. The methodology is then used to estimate the parameters of the models for each shipping route. The analysis of the data yields five separate ARMA models for freight rate and shipping volume alone, as well as three combined models integrating the two variables. The expanded dataset also includes prices for new ships, used ships, and scrapped ships, with the latter two priced relative to new ship prices. The shipping cost structure is discussed in detail, along with the deprecation policy used to calculate the prices for new, used, and scrapped ships. The prices for new, used, and scrapped ships are expressed as the price of a new ship in 1966, allowing direct comparison across all routes. The dataset concludes with the actual shipping cost data for each route, calculated by multiplying shipping volumes by the sum of freight rates and ship costs, and subtracting the revenue from scrapped ships. The shipping cost structure remains unchanged from 1966 to 2009, with the exception of a change in 1980 regarding the depreciation of new ships. The dataset is tested for changes in 1966, 1973, 1980, and 2009, with no actual shifts found in any of these years. The shipping industry is known to be countercyclical, with high freight rates leading to decreased shipping volumes, and low freight rates leading to increased volumes. This behavior is quantified in the combined models, with a 1% change in freight rates resulting in a 4.5% change in volumes in the long run, with no actual shift found in any of the specified years. The dataset and results are available for further research into the shipping industry. The results suggest that the industry operates in a steady state, with the possibility of sudden, large changes occurring with little warning. We establish that the non-cinetic gravity formulation in (a,b)-signature spacetime dimensions d ≥ 3 can accommodate Lagrangians that belong to either the first or second class of Weyl weights, thereby encompassing a broad spectrum of gravity theories including topologically massive, minimal, and new massive gravity within its framework. Additionally, our formulation also yields the corresponding variational conservation laws when supplemented with the FJL formalism. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the cineticy and non-cinetic gravity formulations are distinct and incompatible in d = 2 spacetime dimensions. Furthermore, our research highlights that the cineticy gravity Lagrangian can be reinterpreted as a specific conformally coupled Lagrangian when operating within the FJL formalism framework. Lastly, our study provides an explicit solution to the conformally coupled gravity in the non-cinetic gravity framework.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical object being pulled across a layer of granular material saturated with a viscous liquid, and found that the direction of motion significantly affects the object's speed and required force. When moved parallel to its long axis, the object's movement was impeded by the granular layer more than when moved perpendicular to its axis. Furthermore, this anisotropic drag resulted from the interaction between the object's sides and the granular bed, rather than the interaction between the object's ends and the bed. When attempting to move an end-first, the object would sometimes start moving when pulled from a side, due to the reduced friction with the bed. This led to side friction playing a crucial role in determining the object's speed. The anisotropic nature of the object's movement was also demonstrated using computer simulations of spherical and irregular objects. The anisotropy's extent varied depending on how the objects interacted with the granular bed, but it was always present. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have developed various preservation techniques, such as preserving positivity, conservation laws, or specific physical properties, and these methods often employ suitable spatial and temporal discretizations. Although these discretizations are generally effective, they can be computationally demanding due to the large number of time-dependent equations involved in typical applications. In such cases, iterative time-stepping methods, including the GMRES, are frequently employed but may disrupt the preserved properties of the solution. This study focuses on restoring preserved properties that are lost when using the GMRES in conjunction with spatial discretizations in certain contexts, including both continuous and discrete levels. Specifically, it explores the impact of the GMRES on the preserved properties of the solution and introduces several post-processing techniques based on the residual to regain the preserved characteristics. These techniques can be realized through simple transformations that are equivalent to applying specific multistep methods, which also regaining the desired preservation properties. Furthermore, this study provides an analytical framework for predicting the effectiveness of these post-processing methods, including an assessment of the preserved properties, the residual behavior, and the spectral properties of the preconditioned matrix. In addition, it presents numerical evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of these post-processing methods in various scenarios, including both simple model problems and more complex models with multiple preserving properties. In total, this research develops a range of efficient and structure-preserving time-stepping methods suitable for a broad range of applications involving large-scale time-dependent partial differential equations. In particular, it provides a range of methods suitable for the time-dependent Navier-Stokes equations, the MHD equations, and the Allen-Cahn-Chase-Williams equations. In addition, it makes available an open-source implementation of these methods in the form of the MESA framework. In addition, it also offers a standalone version of the methods suitable for use with the PETSc framework. Soft-tissue navigation is a complex procedure that involves surgeons moving through intricate paths in a short period. The non-rigid registration of three-dimensional volumes acquired during this process from different points in time poses a significant challenge. The common approach to time-dependent image processing assumes images remain static between frame acquisitions, rendering traditional methods ineffective. Furthermore, gold-standard methods that rely on expert opinions are too time-consuming and impractical for real-time applications. In this paper, a novel approach to biomechanical data-driven surface registration is presented, leveraging machine learning to create an efficient and accurate method for guiding surgical interventions. The algorithm comprises two primary components: a data-driven model that utilizes artificial intelligence to predict tissue deformation from previous volume registrations, and a optimization problem that aligns the intrinsic properties of a biomechanical model with the predicted surface to obtain an optimal transformation. This transformation is then applied to the current volume for registration. The proposed technique was evaluated using public datasets and showed superior results in terms of surface-based metrics when compared to existing methods. In addition, a novel assessment of volume-based metrics was introduced to enhance evaluation insights. The technique was also applied to real-world data from a mitral valve surgery, demonstrating potential for clinical utilization. We propose a novel, entirely unsupervised method for predicting scene flow by building on metric learning and a specific network configuration. This approach leverages an extensive, publicly available dataset, including KITTI and Sun3D, to produce a motion trajectory representation that effectively captures the motion information at corresponding points across different views, and we evaluate its performance in tasks that benefit from scene flow, demonstrating the practical value of our predicted scene flow. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance in object classification, shows a significant improvement in unsupervised segmentation, and produces a motion trajectory distribution that complements the geodesic normal estimation method, further enhancing the accuracy of its counterpart. The motion trajectory representation we derived has a compact, 3D structure with 128 elements, and analyzing this structure with different network configurations provides practical predictions for actual applications. In recent times, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. Nevertheless, widespread adoption of such models on the internet is being hindered by their inability to be efficiently translated into hardware. Neuromorphic computing technology, which is capable of this translation, follows a different architecture that is inspired by biological neural networks but lacks the efficiency of traditional hardware in implementing artificial neural networks. This research introduces a novel hybrid approach called the Spiking Random Neural Network (SRN) that combines the efficiency of neuromorphic hardware with the high information processing capacity of artificial neural networks. By allowing some artificial neurons to function as biological equivalents, this model takes advantage of low-energy spike-based hardware. Moreover, this model includes an innovative learning method called Backpropagation Through Time with Spiking Relaxation (BTRS) that enables efficient training within a short period. As a result, SRN demonstrates superior performance in both processing capacity and energy efficiency when compared to competing models. In particular, when implementing a simple MNIST image recognition task, SRN showed a 99.6% accuracy rate and an energy consumption that was over ten times lower than competing models. In addition to this, SRN was found to be capable of solving complex problems, including a 10-class SVM classification task, at a speed that was over a hundred times faster than competing models. In conclusion, the SRN model offers a universally applicable solution for converting any artificial neural network into low-energy, efficient hardware. Nevertheless, this model has a limitation where it cannot be trained with a large number of neurons within a short period due to its complex learning method. This challenge could be addressed by modifying the BTRS method, which in turn could enable the model to be trained for a longer period with a larger number of neurons. This would make the model even more suitable for a wide range of applications. This research is significant because it introduces a novel hybrid model, presents an innovative learning method, and highlights the possibility of modifying this method to meet the needs of more demanding applications. This paper also includes a detailed explanation of the SRN model along with its learning method, a discussion on its limitations, and suggestions on how to modify the learning method to meet the needs of more demanding applications. This research has the potential to open up a new field of research focused on developing efficient and complex neuromorphic hardware capable of efficiently training large-scale artificial neural networks with complex learning methods. This paper introduces a novel, autonomous framework called Timeloops, designed to manage system calls within containerized microservices. System call policies, which define which system calls are permitted or blocked for a container, are typically specified by developers through cumbersome and error-prone means, but they can significantly impact performance and security. In contrast, Timeloops automatically determines these policies by conducting lightweight, randomized testing across different system call permissions, then uses a machine learning-based approach called Policy2Model to derive a system call policy model that can be safely executed without further testing. Not only does this approach streamline development, but it also provides robust security and performance guarantees in production environments. In particular, it offers a 5x reduction in development time and a 90% decrease in system call policy-related security breaches. Furthermore, Timeloops' efficient testing paradigm results in performance improvements of up to 4x. The framework's capabilities are demonstrated through the secure deployment of real-world microservices applications. The system call policy model derived by Timeloops' framework can be executed efficiently, resulting in a 2x decrease in development time when re-deploying containerized microservices. The framework's efficiency and the derived policies' efficiency in reducing system calls result in a 3x decrease in development time when re-deploying containerized microservices. The progression of soccer games follows a non-linear pattern, with games that were initially uneventful suddenly becoming intense in the final minutes. Decisive actions are often taken in these critical situations, and our research aims to improve them. We developed a deep reinforcement learning approach to rate games as either high or low-stakes, and a separate model to prioritize actions that address specific intense situations. By combining these, we can identify the most critical actions to take in each game. Our method demonstrated superior performance in comparison to rival techniques and current soccer strategies. Notably, our approach prioritizes actions that address intense situations in games that were initially uncompetitive, but also encourages caution in games that are already decisive. This is achieved without reference to specific game outcomes, allowing our approach to be applicable to a broad spectrum of soccer games. Our findings have implications for coaches seeking to enhance their decision-making in high-stakes situations and professionals analyzing soccer games for broadcast purposes. Additionally, we highlight a notable instance where our approach advised taking a penalty in a game that seemed initially uneventful.

In order to accurately identify and flag potentially sensitive content, it's essential to effectively detect when generated text has been altered from its original semantic meaning. This task can be challenging due to the inherent ambiguity between intended modifications and unintended changes to the content's semantic context. Our study takes a controlled approach by utilizing a structured framework of context, intent, and semantic alterations, and incorporates a suite of contextualized language models to perform the detection task. We find that the most reliable models in this suite, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, exhibit a tendency to prioritize content over generation guidelines, leading to a bias towards accepting semantic alterations. By taking this bias into account and appropriately adjusting the threshold for accepting altered content, we're able to achieve a significant improvement in our experimental results. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the limited capability of contextualized language models to accurately capture the intent behind generated text, and emphasizes the importance of incorporating additional intent-related features to enhance their performance. Lastly, our study underlines the necessity of employing more sophisticated contextualized language models, such as ALBERT and XLNet, that are capable of better distinguishing between content and generation intentions. We also discover that contextualized language models struggle with capturing the semantic alterations made to a given context, and this shortcoming could be mitigated by employing more advanced contextualized language models, along with the incorporation of additional semantic alteration features. We intend to build upon this research by exploring the use of contextualized language models to detect and flag specific types of semantic alterations made to generated text. We're making our code and data sets publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrasoul/semantic-alteration-detection. We hope this research and our findings will be beneficial to developers of content assessment APIs and other applications requiring the detection of semantic alterations in generated text. We're also open to receiving feedback from these groups, as well as statistical language modeling community members, who may have alternative proposals for addressing this challenge. We believe this challenge has significant implications for the field of natural language processing and machine learning, and we're confident that finding a solution to it could lead to a breakthrough in our understanding of contextualized language models and their limitations. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear migration occurs. While this migration pattern has been observed across various developing brains and spines, the underlying causes behind its different speed layers have remained unexplained. By imaging live zebrafish retina tissue using confocal and two-photon microscopes, we measured the slow movement of cell nuclei in both the central and peripheral retina areas over the course of several hours. Our detailed analysis of these movements reveals a confined, random diffusion model as the underlying mechanism, supported by calculations of diffusion coefficients for different retina regions. Furthermore, our findings suggest a relationship between the distance a nucleus can migrate before returning to its original layer and the local retinal curvature. This connection could have implications for understanding the generation of retinal ganglion cell populations in a curvature-specific pattern. Lastly, our research also explores the possibility that this migration pattern may result from the interplay between a slowly shifting wavefront of cell division and the brain's three-dimensional architecture. A diffusion model provides a feasible explanation for the spatial distribution of randomly migrating nuclei, albeit one that lacks a clear predictive power. A related issue is the uncertain origin of the retinal tissue's layering, with options including a natural phenomenon or the result of specific gene expression patterns governing the movement and division of nuclei. A simple simulation of this process is one possible explanation for the observed pattern, but more comprehensive models incorporating factors like the influence of the brain's surface and the movement of dividing cells are also presented. A quantitative comparison of these models with the available data on retinal tissue formation is conducted, providing an assessment of their fit and suggesting areas for their improvement. A separate analysis of a model featuring a positive feedback loop between the height and the gradient of the retinal surface also yields insights into its dynamics. A notable finding is that this model predicts the existence of a sharp peak at the center of the retina, a feature that can be tested with live imaging. A related problem of estimating the diffusion coefficient from a given surface also contributes to the paper's content. We've developed a precise hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active liquids in $d$ dimensions and demonstrates the existence of a stationary state with non-trivial velocity and disorder-free density, subject to certain constraints. This state is surrounded by an outer region that represents a jammed state with zero velocity and maximum possible disorder, and we've characterized the exact parameters of these states. This is the first time such predictions have been made within the framework of hydrodynamic theories. By subjecting these predictions to numerical testing, we used computer simulations to confirm the validity of the theory in three dimensions. Furthermore, our analysis included an examination of how the velocity and density fluctuations change over time, as well as an assessment of the effectiveness of activity-driven systems in maintaining a steady state when confronted with obstacles. Slightly modifying the simulations to account for spatial variations in activity, we found that the theory also applies to situations with spatial activity disparities. This method involves employing a contrastive loss function to match untrained data from a new task by generating synthetic data from untrained examples, which enhances the representation of that data. When tested on a dataset for self-supervised change detection, this method demonstrated superior outcomes compared to baseline methods. Moreover, when applied to real-world out-of-domain few-shot learning problems, it showed a notable increase in classification accuracy compared to other state-of-the-art methods. The model was also discovered to excel in a challenging scenario known as "one-shot horror," where it demonstrated a notable increase in performance compared to other methods. The code for this project has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghru/retouch. The dataset created for testing the model's cross-task generalization capabilities has also been made available at https://ghru.github.io/retouch-data. The code and created datasets are intended to facilitate further research and improvement on this novel idea.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of efficient methods for hyperparameter tuning in private learning has been hindered by the lack of information about the optimal hyperparameters for a given level of privacy protection, which is directly related to the size of the dataset used in private learning. In this paper, a novel approach is proposed for determining the optimal batch size and number of epochs in private learning without relying on dataset information. Furthermore, the proposed method includes a straightforward strategy for hyperparameter tuning in private learning through the optimization of a single variable using a dataset in a private manner. The proposed approach and related baselines are evaluated and compared using a range of popular datasets for image and text classification. The results show that the proposed method delivers superior performance compared to the baseline methods in nearly all the datasets tested. In particular, the proposed method is found to be particularly effective in delivering superior performance when the dataset is relatively small. The proposed method is also found to be capable of providing accurate predictions in a private manner on larger datasets, which includes the large CIFAR10 dataset of 50,000 training images. The proposed method is also compared with the non-private approach and found to be capable of delivering performance that is within 3% of the non-private approach on smaller datasets of 10,000 training images but less than 10% on larger datasets of 50,000 training images. The proposed method is also compared with the state-of-the-art method known as Differentially Private Hyperparameter Tuning and found to be capable of delivering superior performance in nearly all the datasets tested. The results of the paper are released as a dataset of 72 reconstructed learning curves. The proposed method is also discussed in terms of the various limitations and possible enhancements required to take full advantage of the method in particular situations. The proposed method is also demonstrated to be capable of providing accurate predictions in a private manner on complex networks such as the large text classification network known as BERT. The proposed method is also capable of delivering superior performance when used with the state-of-the-art privacy-enhanced deep learning algorithm known as PADDLE. The proposed method is also discussed in terms of its theoretical underpinnings in relation to the optimal hyperparameters for a given level of privacy protection, which is directly related to the size of the dataset used in private learning. We believe that understanding how these systems work, as they often incorporate complex logical principles, can be achieved by mapping their components and interactions. One such atlas, dubbed "ATOMIC," serves as a foundation for examining the inner workings of neural networks in the context of logical reasoning. It consists of three main sections: the first describes the network's input/output relationships, the second explores the intermediate representations, and the third section is dedicated to inferring the underlying logical principles. To enhance data efficiency in speech recognition, a method is proposed to integrate speech and text models through a bidirectional attention mechanism in a multi-modal encoder. This encoder employs two attention mechanisms, one drawing information from the speech signal and another from the language model, allowing for the exchange of features between the two modalities. This exchange enables the encoder to combine the encoder's own speech and text encodings, producing a more comprehensive and diverse set of encodings that includes both speech and text information. These encodings are then input into a linear layer to generate the mean and standard deviation for a fully factorial variational autoencoder. This results in a latent space with a Gaussian distribution that is factored by the dimensions, facilitating efficient sampling from the distribution to produce the mean and log of the standard deviation for the next decoder's input. This standard deviation is then input into a reparameterization layer to sample the latent vector, which is then input into the decoder. This decoder consists of a convolutional neural network that generates the log of probabilities for the next token in the sequence. This proposed method was tested on the Librispeech corpus and the Google Speech Dataset, and the results showed an improvement in the word error rate (WER) to 4.5% on the "clean" set of the Librispeech corpus and 24.5% on the Google Speech Dataset. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses can vary significantly with different ventilation patterns, leading us to explore a quantitative air flow model to better understand and quantify this risk. We developed a simplified model focusing on forward airflow, which we found to be prevalent in typical bus ventilation systems, and calculated the transmission risk it poses for passengers. However, our findings suggest this model overestimates the degree of mixing within a bus and therefore tends to underestimate the transmission risk it implies. As a result, we advise using a more conservative estimate based on existing research on airborne transmission risk. Ultimately, our analysis underscores the importance of precise, individually tailored assessments to ensure a safe and low-risk transmission environment on buses. We also highlight the value of conducting similar investigations for other enclosed spaces with varying air flow dynamics. Ultimately, a one-size-fits-all approach to mixing in these settings is likely to be inaccurate. We believe a key factor influencing transmission risk is often overlooked, and we urge researchers to consider it in their studies. It is essential to note that our analysis focuses solely on forward airflow and does not address reverse airflow, which could pose an even greater transmission risk. In fact, one bus driver reported switching to backward airflow to improve visibility, which would likely increase the transmission risk even further. Similarly, any similar ventilation systems in other enclosed spaces could have a similar impact. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the optimal Lipschitz constant for a neural network, considering its structure and training data. Our findings, obtained through various experiments with different datasets, demonstrate that imposing a limited Lipschitz constant via optimization results in improved classification accuracy, especially when neural networks are overfitting. Additionally, we found that a connection exists between the ReLU neural network's optimal Lipschitz constant and its deepest layer, which allows for the calculation of a default constant without knowledge of the training data. This default constant can be used to enhance performance in problems involving limited data. Our proposed method also succeeds in preventing extreme overfitting, thus making it an alternative to regularization techniques like dropout. Our model training involves an efficient algorithm with a low computational cost, enabled by a significant speedup of the optimization process compared to standard approaches. Our experiments with large datasets, such as ResNet on ImageNet, demonstrate outstanding performance. Our model, which includes a specialized version of a generative adversarial network-based training method, also succeeds in reducing vanishing and exploding gradients during the training process. Our work on analyzing non-integer Lipschitz continuity's effects discovered that it can be used to prevent gradient explosion and vanishing, while also promoting smoother decision boundaries and more robust performance. We investigate the possibility of a new, highly massive vector leptoquark being discovered through the Drell-Yan process in third-generation quark pair production. Calculations of next-to-leading order QCD corrections in combination with leading-order particle showers in hadron collisions are performed, and our results are compared with existing studies of similar processes. For a range of masses from 500 to 3500 GeV, our findings include: (1) accurate predictions through combined next-to-leading order particle showers in hadron collisions, (2) reliable estimates of theoretical uncertainties, (3) distinctive peak regions in mass reconstruction distributions, and (4) guidelines for distinguishing the vector leptoquark signal from background processes involving top quark pairs and W bosons. The minimum amount of data required for discovery and background subtraction is approximately 5-10 fb^-1 in the LHC at a 7 TeV proton collision energy, and our results also apply to 5 TeV and 14 TeV collision scenarios. The vector leptoquark can be confidently identified in 14 TeV collisions, with masses above 2500 GeV distinguishable in data sets of 100 pb^-1. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets that closely resemble real-world data, leading to limited practical applicability. We developed a novel neural network, capable of processing a wide range of PET scans, including those with extremely low doses outside its training parameters. This neural network prioritizes efficient use of high-quality PET images and incorporates uncertainty estimates to prioritize critical features. It demonstrates enhanced performance in enhancing PET images across a broad spectrum of doses in the Center for Translational Research (CTR) dataset. Furthermore, we showed that this neural network can be effectively trained on significantly smaller datasets, reducing the need for vast amounts of training data. We also presented an efficient method for evaluating this neural network's generalization to low-dose PET images outside its training parameters. This method evaluates the neural network's performance on a hypothetical low-dose PET image by analyzing the corresponding high-dose PET image used in its training. We found this neural network capable of enhancing PET images at doses as low as 20% of the original dose, with image quality comparable to higher doses. This research paves the way for reducing PET scan doses while maintaining image quality. The novel neural network and evaluation method we presented can be applied to similar problems involving uncertainty-aware and out-of-distribution data. We open-source our code and data examinations to facilitate further inquiry into the centering theory and coreference resolution.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for research facilities that utilize multiple passes through a linear accelerator. Unlike traditional linear accelerators, the repeating structure of a dielectric linear accelerator presents an additional complication due to beam interaction with each accelerating cell, no matter how many times the beam passes through. This study investigates the complex relationship between beam charge distribution and dielectric linear accelerators that experience beam interaction in every cell, highlighting the impact of cell design on beam charge oscillations and subsequently the beam breakup instability. By analyzing cell designs that minimize beam charge oscillations, this study demonstrates a feasible pathway for increasing the charge that can be safely accelerated in a dielectric linear accelerator. Moreover, this research identifies key design parameters that influence the cell's effectiveness and recommends specific filling patterns that can enhance the stability of the accelerator. By taking the unique characteristics of cell design into account, this study offers a more precise framework for evaluating the beam breakup instability in dielectric linear accelerators and provides a critical step towards developing a comprehensive analytical tool for optimizing cell design and filling patterns in energy recovery linacs. This research has implications not just for energy recovery linacs but also other types of particle accelerators that incorporate repeating structures and can be extended to other phenomena affected by similar nonlinear dynamics. This study has been conducted as part of the development of the LPAQ code, a specialized simulator for linear accelerators that incorporates realistic cell design and filling patterns. This code can be used to develop fast detectors and optimized filling patterns for a wide range of applications and has been successfully utilized in the design of the 12 GHz photocathode gun used in the PAL 4GeV accelerator. Previously excluded areas in symmetrical, two-dimensional and spherical geometries have a specific relationship with the grafting density and mean radius. In this study, we generalize this relationship for brushes of any complex geometry, establishing a direct correlation between a brush's volume and the excluded area in each dimension. This connection enables the calculation of the free energy of strongly stretched brushes in any given shape. Additionally, we demonstrate that the free energy of these brushes can be simplified to a quadratic form, mirroring the results found in earlier, one-dimensional and two-dimensional analyses. This new understanding also provides a more precise interpretation of recent NMR and SANS experiments. The introduction of a curved surface brush model further sheds light on the recent synthesis of brush-like geometries observed in technical applications. Theoretical predictions of strongly stretched brush geometries have also been validated through the analysis of experimental graphs. The free energy of these brushes can also be compared to those obtained from numerical renormalization group methods, offering a broader understanding of the parameters that influence their stretching. The introduction of a curved surface brush model has also been used to explain the formation of hyperbranched structures when brushes are stretched in multiple directions. The possible occurrence of these complex geometries in technical and biological systems will also be explored. The development of a strongly stretched brush model in any given geometry provides the foundation for the understanding of hyperbranched structures and offers the possibility of scaling this model to hyperbranched geometries in three-dimensional spaces. The metric dimension of a graph measures the minimum number of markers required to uniquely identify vertices within the graph. By expanding on this concept, the trimmed metric dimension of a graph determines the minimum number of markers needed to exclude at most one vertex from being identified, while distinctly identifying all other vertices. Here, we establish the equivalence of the trimmed metric dimension to maximum independent subdomination number in graphs, uncover the relationship between the trimmed and classical metric dimensions, and investigate specific polynomial structures that serve as benchmarks. Moreover, we provide computational approaches for determining the trimmed metric dimension and compare them against existing metrics, along with an examination of the trimmed metric dimension of particular graph sequences. Lastly, we pose two conjectures on the relationship between the trimmed and classical metric dimensions.

We developed an open-source framework called Fermi-ML to swiftly create highly sophisticated models for interpreting all-sky gamma-ray data with the Fermi Large Area Telescope. This approach leverages machine learning to build a detailed sky map of constant sources and background fluctuations across the entire sky observable with Fermi. We demonstrate that using just six years of data, our model can accurately replicate the observed count map and spectrum with substantial improvements over existing methods. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that approximately 13% of the sources currently recorded in the third catalog of EGRET-targeted sources remain unaccounted for in the 11-year all-sky data with Fermi, suggesting that a significant fraction, possibly up to 30%, could consist of transient or low-frequency variable sources. We highlight specific sources exhibiting notable brightness fluctuations over the analyzed period and recommend targeted observations for some with soft X-ray and radio facilities. We have made Fermi-ML an open-source platform to facilitate collaborative development and incorporate user-submitted sources for the Fermi Sky Model Repository. For the aforementioned unaccounted sources, we provide reproducible analysis code along with sky maps and data sessions on the Fermi-ML website.

We searched the all-sky photometric data from the Pan-STARRS1 survey for the binary asters phenomenon, where a single star appears as two in a contact binary star system due to surface scintillation. Our method involved analyzing 430,000 stars with high photometric accuracy across six color bands and identifying those exhibiting the binary asters phenomenon in panoramic images. We determined the most favorable conditions for this phenomenon to occur and found that it affects more stars with brighter magnitudes. Furthermore, we found that the phenomenon is more prevalent in the $g$-band than in other color bands and that its occurrence is independent of the angular separation between stars. We developed a machine learning-based algorithm to automate the detection of binary asters and validated it by comparing it with a simpler approach using traditional criteria. Our analysis suggests that the phenomenon is more frequent in the $g$-band due to the higher sensitivity of this band to surface scintillation. We also explored the relationship between the phenomenon and the Eddington factor but found it to be unrelated. Consequently, we used the best detection method to search for binary asters across the Pan-STARRS1 survey in the $g$-band alone and obtained a dataset of approximately 1400 candidate stars exhibiting this phenomenon. We made this dataset publicly available. The data we obtained can be utilized to create a catalog of highly reliable stars exhibiting surface scintillation-induced binary asters in the Pan-STARRS1 survey. The prevalence of this phenomenon among G-type main-sequence stars in the solar neighborhood is found to be 1 in 360 based on our analysis. The validity of this estimate can be further assessed with additional observations. The dataset we created can also serve as a standard for comparing similar searches in other surveys. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which must be inferred from limited information. To support further exploration, a team has created the G4C-Dataset, comprising conversations centered around the Dungeons and Dragons theme. Unlike conventional conversation datasets, the G4C-Dataset assesses a model's capacity to follow a set of pre-defined guidelines, interpret the thoughts and intentions of a conversation partner, and make decisions about the next adventure scenario. To evaluate the models' performance, we develop a quantitative assessment method that combines multiple factors, including how closely their decisions align with the specified objectives and the coherence of the resulting adventure scenarios. Compared to alternative evaluation methods, our approach demonstrates a clear distinction between higher and lower performing models. Our analysis of model performance also reveals that both the coherence and intention-inference aspects can be distinguished from each other, and that the intention-inference alone does not guarantee coherence in the resulting scenarios. Finally, we show that a model capable of D&D gameplay does not necessarily excel at the level of general natural language interaction. Our research is ongoing, and we invite other teams to participate in the challenge and enhance the G4C-Dataset further. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their functional flexibility is an area that researchers are still trying to fully understand. Recent studies have shown that the spatial arrangement of knotted proteins is linked to specific bending patterns, but more analysis is needed to uncover these patterns and shed light on the relationship between knot structure and protein dynamics. In this study, we used magnetic resonance and mass spectrometry to map the conformation and chemistry of six knotted proteins and applied topological analysis to identify distinct bending pathways associated with their native states. By integrating these results with existing data on linear proteins, our findings reveal a distinct grouping of knotted proteins based on their bending patterns and chemistry, and demonstrate how topological methods can be used to select specific bending pathways from a complex and disordered population of protein states. This research paves the way for a deeper understanding of how protein knots influence their flexibility and provides a novel approach for using topological methods to explore the complex geometry of disordered populations. This approach can be applied to other biomolecular assemblies that are knotted, as well as other fields that involve the analysis of complex, embedded spaces. This study is also accompanied by an interactive three-dimensional visualization of the knotted proteins discussed in this research. This visualization was created using the tool, Coevolve. These constructs, common in spoken language, describe situations where elements of a phrase hold true while others do not. Despite their prevalence, hypotheticals of this type are challenging to incorporate into supervised learning models due to the lack of corresponding actual phrasal data. In our research, we take a non-parallel approach to incorporating phrasal hypotheticals into our models by employing a contrastive learning method called Disentangled Semantic Contrast (DSC). Under this framework, two input phrases with a single differing element are pushed in opposite directions by a contrastive loss function with no requirement for corresponding actual data. We utilize DSC to train a pre-conditioning model, which is then used to generate counterfactual data from a diverse set of text prompts. Our evaluation, conducted using automated assessment tools, reveals that this counterfactual data is indistinguishable from genuine actual data. We believe this technique has broader applications in NLP as it provides a method for generating diverse counterfactual data across any domain. In the context of phrasal hypotheticals, we employ this data to train a language model that accurately predicts the altered element of a hypothetical construct. Our findings indicate that a strong language model pre-trained on large amounts of text can be sufficiently fine-tuned to predict the element that differs in a phrasal hypothetical with minimal additional training. In the context of our primary research question, this equates to a yes answer. We also explore and what sorts of phrases this model excels at predicting, discovering that it has a preference for predicting phrases with action verbs. In the process, we develop the necessary tools to assess a language model's ability to predict a specific domain of phrasal hypotheticals. These tools, referred to as the Phrasal Hypothetical Assessment, determine the accuracy with which a model can predict the altered element of a hypothetical construct following additional training on the specific domain. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene is hindered due to the lack of a suitable substrate for comparison. This study uses hexagonal boron nitride as a reference to examine the epitaxial behavior of gold Heusler alloy films during physical vapor deposition. It is determined that increasing deposition temperature switches the epitaxial mode from van der Waals to remote or pinhole epitaxy, ultimately leading to the formation of large grains. Notably, this mode switching is independent of substrate defects, with intrinsic grain formation observed on clean graphene surfaces. Conversely, fast film growth at low temperatures favors small grains with aligned orientations, indicative of direct interaction between the film and the graphene substrate. This finding suggests that clean graphene surfaces can act as templates for self-assembly in remote epitaxy. Further study into the films reveals that the lack of lattice matching does not prevent lattice matching between the film and graphene, leading to a range of mismatch configurations and opening up possibilities for remote epitaxy on other 2D substrates. Ultimately, this work paves the way for controlling film growth on monolayer graphene and other 2D materials through physical vapor deposition.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose. However, accurate identification of heart sounds from recordings affected by background noise and poor sound quality poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, machine learning techniques, particularly deep learning models, have been successfully employed to automate heart sound categorization. Yet, training such models to recognize heart sounds from poorly recorded data remains difficult. In this study, we trained a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to categorize heart sounds based on four categories: normal heart sounds, stenotic heart sounds, mitral heart sounds, and atrial heart sounds. We tested the network's performance on recordings with different levels of background noise and varying degrees of distortion caused by poor sound transmission through the stethoscope. Our results showed that the CNN can accurately identify heart sounds even in the presence of background noise and low-frequency distortion caused by the stethoscope. Moreover, by retraining the network on data with specific noise profiles, we significantly improved its performance. Our findings suggest that this CNN can be effectively trained to perform well on data collected with a particular sound transmission device and can be applied to detect heart conditions from recordings obtained with a different device, but only after retraining. Our results also compare the CNN's performance to that of features extraction using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), highlighting the advantage of deep learning techniques in this task. Our work was accomplished using a dataset collected from cardiac auscultation recordings with background noise and low-frequency distortion caused by the stethoscope, but the methodology we employed can be applied to other datasets collected from recordings with different noise profiles. In the end, we conclude by suggesting that this CNN can be employed as a pre-processing module to clean heart sound recordings, making them more suitable for machine learning-based classification systems. Our code is available for public use on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/HeartSoundGroup/CNN-Heart-Sound-Categorization.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like fitness trackers and smart wristbands allows for continuous health data collection for individuals. Nonetheless, processing this data on central servers raises significant concerns about data privacy. A genuinely decentralized, secure approach to analyzing this data is possible through Federated Learning. Nonetheless, training machine learning models on this data within a federated framework poses difficulties because of the limited amount of data available for model updates at each device. FedHealth seeks to address this challenge by introducing a method for transferring knowledge within a federated framework that accounts for class balance. This results in a way to train machine learning models that are both secure and accurate. Our proposed DNA-storage system addresses two challenges that have hindered the practical use of DNA data storage. Firstly, despite the progress made in accurately synthesizing DNA sequences, the cost of constructing long sequences with low error rates remains excessively high, making it difficult to efficiently represent large amounts of data with binary values. Our solution to this problem involves reinterpreting the way data is encoded directly into DNA sequences, bypassing the need for binary representations. This approach allows for the use of existing DNA synthesis technologies, enabling the efficient storage of significantly larger amounts of data in a comparable amount of time. Secondly, existing solutions for correcting errors in DNA sequences through Hamming codes fail to address the difficulty of reversing these codes efficiently, a problem that is compounded by the difficulty of performing bit-wise operations on large sequences of data. Our system overcomes this challenge by developing a method for efficiently decoding these codes using sequence alignment techniques that can handle large scales, a breakthrough that also enables the practical use of insertions and deletions in coding. Finally, our system tackles two additional challenges facing DNA data storage: the difficulty of updating individual bits within encoded sequences and the absence of efficient methods for creating hierarchical structures from these sequences. Our solution to these problems involves integrating a compact hierarchical labeling system directly into the data encoding process, a design that also enables the efficient update of individual bits within encoded sequences. The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, showing that it can efficiently compress encoded sequences, update individual bits quickly, and store significantly more data in a comparable amount of time. Specifically, our data suggests that this approach can compress encoded sequences by up to 5 times, update individual bits in as little as 0.6 seconds, and store as much as 270 megabytes of data in a comparable amount of time. Causal deep learning, a field that draws on the principles of both causal and deep learning, is encountering an infusion of innovative techniques from advanced machine learning, leading to a surge of ground-breaking research and applications. As a result, the term "causal deep learning" is becoming increasingly popular, with a significant rise in publications and funding. However, the underlying dynamics of this field are shifting, with many referring to it simply as deep learning, and the distinct origins of its methodology are being overlooked. If the distinct roots of causal deep learning are ignored, it may lose its identity and the unique problems it addresses may be misclassified under general deep learning, leading to a lack of targeted funding and an overextension of its methodologies. Furthermore, this movement raises important questions about the way research is referred to, credited, and compensated within the field of machine learning. With an estimated 70% of deep learning being inherently causal, and the rapid incorporation of new deep learning techniques into causal research, it is essential to address these issues now to ensure the continued advancement and distinction of causal deep learning.

This work extends Golay complementary matrices to Golay complementary arrays in all spatial dimensions and identifies design requirements. Furthermore, it presents non-exhaustive sets of waveplate pairs that can form GCA's when paired in a specific configuration. Specifically, in three-dimensional space, one such set consists of GCA's with sizes $4\times4$, $6\times6$, and $8\times8$. This work was presented at the IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing in 2022.

Complex systems consisting of interconnected components typically exhibit intricate behaviors. Due to the vast number of elements and their connections, modeling these systems is challenging, especially when attempting to capture dynamic properties. Existing methods often focus on small systems with few components, relying on linear techniques to analyze them. In contrast, this work divides complex systems into two components: intricate structures represented by graph neural networks and time-series dynamics covered by ARIMAs. By separating these components, we can easily expand our models to include more elements, even when some components become inactive. Furthermore, this approach enables the detection of anomalies when new elements join the system or some drop out. If data on inactive components is available, this method can also recover them. If not, it suggests an approach to approximate them. Additionally, this work offers guidelines for properly constructing the model, including deciding on the number of elements, determining whether some components are inactive, and recovering missing elements when data on them is available. By employing our method on a simple linear example and a nonlinear case with hidden variables, as well as real-world data on a brain network, our approach is demonstrated to be effective in recovering missing elements, detecting inactive components, and identifying anomalies. This work also highlights the distinction between open and isolated systems, stressing that modeling isolated systems as open systems can yield more general and dynamic models. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for problem representation, featuring a clear and intuitive syntax. However, determining the precise meaning of GP 2 expressions can be challenging due to their rich structure and varied concepts. GP 2 expressions comprise interconnected graphs of variables, constants, logical operators, and function applications, including recursive definitions. In contrast, the standard approach to handling GP 2 expresses them as terms in a first-order logic with function symbols and their corresponding sorts. Yet, this method overlooks crucial aspects of the GP 2 syntax, including commas in function signatures and the distinction between infix and prefix operators. As a result, multiple GP 2 expressions can map to the same term, complicating tasks like evaluating expressions, solving for unknown variables, and checking the validity of formulas against GP 2 theories. To address these difficulties, we developed the GP 2 compiler, a tool that translates GP 2 expressions into a more explicit and standardized form called the internal format. This format retains all the details from the original GP 2 expressions, and we provide algorithms for performing tasks like variable substitution and checking formula validity against GP 2 theories on this internal representation. Additionally, the GP 2 compiler includes a feature to enhance GP 2 expressions by adding implicit parentheses and distinguishing prefixes from infixes, making it a valuable resource for developers working with GP 2. The GP 2 compiler is now an open-source tool available under the permissive Apache License 2.0. The internal format it uses and the algorithms for performing tasks on this format are also part of the public domain. The compiler can be used directly through the command line or integrated into other programs using the C API it provides. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, remains underexplored. We propose the LLM should incorporate a triple-based injection method, utilizing a knowledge graph's structured elements to enhance its performance. The knowledge graph's entities should be represented as part of the input token, allowing the model to learn from both contextual text and the knowledge graph's structured information. We introduce a knowledge graph injection method, subsequently training the LLM to produce desirable outcomes. Our proposed approach demonstrates improved performance when utilizing knowledge graphs in tasks such as text classification and knowledge verification. Specifically, our results indicate a 4.3% improvement in accuracy when utilizing the Yelp knowledge graph in a text-based classification task and 11.9% when verifying knowledge within the Freebase graph. Consequently, injecting structured information from knowledge graphs into LLMs offers a practical and efficient means of training them on large-scale, complex datasets. The resulting model and associated code are available online at github.com/THUDM/SKILL.

360-degree live-streaming videos require a predicted viewpoint to stream and reduce unnecessary data transmission, but predicting this viewpoint ahead of time is challenging, especially for videos featuring complex, dynamic scenes. In 360-degree virtual tourism videos, the viewpoint prediction problem can be simplified by focusing on the direction of interest, as the host typically focuses on specific attractions within the video. Despite this simpler problem, existing approaches, which primarily use visual features for prediction, have not been able to surpass random guessing. We propose a novel method that employs speech titles, easily obtainable metadata, to predict the direction of interest. By matching the spoken content to pre-trained embedding models, a numerical representation of the direction of interest is obtained, which is then used to guide the viewpoint prediction. Our method performs significantly better than random guessing and existing non-speech-based approaches, demonstrating the beneficial impact of incorporating speech titles in 360-degree live-streaming video prediction applications. The proposed method, which utilizes speech titles for prediction, also introduces a novel task: speech title generation for 360-degree virtual tourism videos, which we found challenging to frame within the existing research context. Nonetheless, we believe it to be a significant problem worth exploring, and have provided preliminary research on it by simply generating concise speech titles via Markov chains without delusion, a technique that indirectly uses the video's numerical representation to guide the speech title generation process. Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized to model and efficiently compute the dynamics of 1D systems in their equilibrium or non-equilibrium scenarios. However, incorporating imaginary time temperature dependencies or certain fast-time-dependence into the network's vertices has presented a challenge due to the need for global precision in approximating the entire network. This issue can be overcome by employing a local tensor network framework, which focuses on approximating the actual physical state through a network of limited size, with temperature or time entered directly into the network's vertices. This approach enables seamless treatment of temperature or time dependencies within the network's vertices, bypassing the need for a global, precise network. Moreover, it has the added benefit of significantly reducing the network's size and associated computational costs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to the computation of thermal expectations in the Ising model and the time-evolution of Heisenberg spin chains. The resulting algorithm is found to be substantially more efficient while still accurately capturing the underlying physics. This local network method can be further modified to incorporate renormalization group networks, providing a valuable tool for researching the RG's impact on thermal states and time-dependence within local networks. Additionally, this method has the potential to be translated into experimental parameters, enabling the direct analysis of equilibrium and time-dependence phenomena through microscopy or other mean-field probes. This approach has the potential to be generalized for use with other models and may be particularly beneficial for modeling and analyzing certain transport phenomena.

Reusing existing artificial neural networks that have been trained on a vast amount of data is an appealing idea to reduce the necessity for enormous amounts of information for training a new, specific task. Typically, this involves using the network as a feature extractor, but it can also be employed as a black-box model for classification without accessing its internal workings. However, transferring knowledge from these models when no data is available for the new task poses a significant challenge. In this research, we present a method that enables the transfer of knowledge from a black-box model with no need for the training data for the target task. It achieves this by inferring the relationship between the model's classifications and the desired output for a new task, which was outside the scope of the model's original training. This relationship is represented as a simple mathematical formula that can be applied to make predictions on new data for the target task. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through experiments on multiple datasets and models, with the results showing that our method is comparable to feature-based transfer and outperforms decision-based transfer. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/ghush/zero-shot-transfer. Additionally, we created a tool for transferring knowledge to pre-trained models that can be used through a user-friendly interface at https://zero-shot-transfer.com/. The code and tool are compatible with TensorFlow, PyTorch, and ONNX models. The method we presented is versatile and suitable for any model and dataset. The estimate that it takes approximately 500 examples to train a decision-based model is supported by an analysis of the relationship between the model's classifications and the desired output, as well as the results of experiments on multiple datasets. This is because the lattice's structure is determined by exponential-sized information, specifically polynomial ideals, which are difficult to infer from the module's basic properties, especially in computationally intensive scenarios. In the case of representation theory, researchers have successfully developed methods to accurately determine the lattice structure for specific types of modules, often utilizing combinatorial and geometric techniques. However, these approaches are generally confined to modules with a limited number of dimensions. We demonstrate this approach with an example involving a module from the quantum group Uq(g) (q being a scalar), specifically forming the lattice of submodules of a module associated with the root system A2, which has a complex structure that cannot be determined through traditional representation theory alone. Reinforcement learning for complex and hazardous tasks often poses significant challenges, mainly due to the risk of physical accidents and costly errors. Reaching out to seasoned professionals for guidance through interactive learning can mitigate these difficulties; however, this approach requires an infeasible amount of time and expenses and isn't always accessible. Our research introduces a novel framework called SiMPLe, that leverages the combined potential of imitative and imitational learning to efficiently master high-risk tasks. Within the SiMPLe framework, a teacher learns to maximize the student's long-term reward while a student learns both imitatively and exploratively. Our approach is tested on a challenging helicopter navigation problem and the results show that SiMPLe surpasses non-imitative and non-interactive baselines, also achieving comparable outcomes to highly specialized experts with 10 times less training data. This paper proposes a metric called the "effective pairwise and quadriplets distance" that distinguishes one code from another, surpassing the distinction provided by pairwise and quadriplets distance. We also establish an inequality linking this new metric with codeword distance and identify which codes achieve the minimum distance under this new standard. Furthermore, this new metric offers a basis for defining a coding error and calculates the probability of this error for specific coding scenarios. Lastly, our research reveals that, for large letter sets, the best codes under this new standard are identical to those identified as optimal in previous research.

Evaluating the best action sequence in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) amounts to a long-term optimization problem. Since the set of possible actions in the source string is vast, using the full set as a search space is computationally infeasible. Our solution exploits the observation that competent NMT models typically generate word sequences that adhere to the constraints of the source string. We therefore propose a direct method of evaluating the next action in the sequence, drawing inspiration from policy-based reinforcement learning. By focusing on the upcoming actions, our model prioritizes the easier parts of the translation task, such as expanding existing phrases, rather than attempting difficult aspects like synthesizing the beginning of the sequence. Our evaluation reveals that this policy-based approach, when combined with a carefully selected initialization, leads to the creation of high-quality translation sequences. We further explore the application of our model to challenging translation initiation by incorporating world knowledge, demonstrating the potential to incorporate external knowledge about the world to facilitate easier parts of the translation task. We also examine the use of our model to facilitate the harder initiation of sentence sequences, demonstrating the potential to treat the easier parts of the sequence initiation as a sub-problem. We explore how several key concepts, including over-expansions, thinness, and the absence of a neighborhood, can be employed to establish the existence of specific types of biharmonic hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space. Specifically, our findings demonstrate the existence of biharmonic hypersurfaces that are over-expansive, minimal hypersurfaces with non-minimal boundary components, and hypersurfaces without which are not thin at infinity. Additionally, our work provides examples of mean curvature-tuple biharmonic hypersurfaces with distinct curvature properties. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between certain biharmonic hypersurfaces and their image under a specific transformation, known as the reverse stereographic projection. This projection transformation enables us to examine the biharmonic hypersurfaces as submanifolds within the unit sphere rather than the hyperbolic space. This in turn allows us to employ techniques from the hyperbolic space to study biharmonic hypersurfaces within the Euclidean space. This research builds upon the existing knowledge presented in the biharmonic hypersurfaces monograph, and complements the results found in the over-expansive hypersurfaces, thin hypersurfaces at infinity, and mean curvature-tuple hypersurfaces chapters. Lastly, this work has been reviewed and is an addition to the monographs on the minimal hypersurfaces, and the hypersurfaces without which are not thin at infinity.

Given a rational number p/q, we say a set A is p/q-identifiable if it can be distinguished from the empty set using p true statements about Q and q false statements about Q, where each statement about Q is true for some multiple fraction within a given interval and false for another interval. Our main observation shows that when the denominator of p/q is two, being p/q-identifiable is the same as being decidable. Additionally, we find p/q-identifiable sets for all even denominators greater than two and demonstrate that there are rationally identifiable sets for every odd denominator greater than one. Finally, we establish that being p/q-identifiable is equivalent to being (p,g) or (g,p)-identifiable for any rational number p/g.

We investigated the solar wind energy flux within the inner heliosphere using data from the Solar Wind Electrodynamics Investigation - Radio Frequency unit on board Parker Solar Probe, specifically looking at data from 12 to 40 solar radii from the sun's center. The measurements were made under nearly radial trajectories near the equator and covered a nine-month time period in 2017 and 2018. The research focused on outcomes from a statistical analysis that accounted for variations in the solar wind speed and density, and allowed for comparisons with similar data from the Ulysses mission in the outer heliosphere. Fraudulent activities have evolved significantly with the advent of blockchain technology, enabling con artists to exploit peer-to-peer networks with relative impunity. This research delves into the intricate workings of Forsage, a prominent and enduring phishing operation that has prospered on Ethereum and other similar platforms. By gaining an in-depth understanding of Forsage's complex, multi-tiered structure, we discovered numerous illegal activities, including operating an unlicensed casino, engaging in binary recruitment scams, and contravening money laundering regulations. Furthermore, our analysis identified Forsage's various escape routes, including attempts to evade detection and conceal illicit funds within phony charitable donations. By examining Forsage's intricate mechanisms, this study uncovers valuable insights for law enforcement agencies seeking to combat similar schemes and provides a framework for identifying similar phishing operations. Moreover, our research highlights the difficulties in preventing such scams and the need for more advanced methods to detect and counter them. By exploring the statistical aspects of Forsage's participant network, we also identified key factors that contributed to its survival and growth. This research was conducted by the Rutgers University Cybersecurity and Dependable Computing Laboratory in collaboration with the US Federal Bureau of Investigation.

Deep-learning methods have recently been applied to process analysis and forecasting within the field of Business Process Management (BPM). Although BPM and BPMN structures provide a well-defined framework, they lack explicit linking to input and output data. This deficiency makes it difficult to treat process analysis and forecasting as conventional classification or regression problems. To overcome this challenge, researchers have successfully employed techniques such as graph neural networks, based on the process's underlying architecture, without directly utilizing input and output ports. In our research, we explored three deep-learning techniques - Graph Attention Network, Graph Convolutional Neural Network, and Reinforcement Learning - to forecast duration distributions in business processes. We tested these methods on real-world data sets and compared their performance to established benchmarks. Our findings provide valuable insights into the effectiveness of different techniques for process forecasting and highlight opportunities for further innovation in this area. In particular, we show that processes with distinct paths and varying completion probabilities offer opportunities for improving techniques like Graph Convolutional Neural Network and Graph Attention Network, while processes characterized by iterative patterns provide a suitable application for Reinforcement Learning. In addition to forecasting, we also demonstrated the capabilities of deep-learning methods for detecting process attributes and predicting process outcomes, which can be used for process selection and recommendation. Ultimately, our research contributes to the development of process analysis and forecasting using deep-learning methods without directly utilizing input and output ports. It also provides a framework for evaluating and comparing different deep-learning techniques for process attribute detection, process outcome prediction, and process forecasting. This framework can be employed by researchers and practitioners to assess the performance of newly introduced techniques on real-world data sets. In the course of our investigation, we encountered several challenges related to process data preprocessing, process attribute detection, process outcome prediction, and process forecasting, some of which can be addressed by further developing and refining deep-learning methods. We hope that our research will encourage more widespread adoption of deep-learning techniques in BPM and BPMN and open up new areas for innovation in process data preprocessing, attribute detection, and outcome prediction. The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration the dispersal of microbial life forms, comets, and asteroids as they travel through space and time, and a focus is placed on identifying the most suitable environments where this phenomenon would be noticeable. By examining various conditions such as the length of time a microbe can survive outside a host planet, the speed at which life-bearing comets move, and the frequency of which comets interact with planetary surfaces, a key finding emerges - only situations where life-bearing particles are repeatedly collided with a planet in a small star cluster allow this indication of interstellar panspermia to become apparent. Based on this discovery, estimates can be made for how often life transfer occurs in a given star cluster and the average time it takes for a microbe to be transferred from one planet to another. Furthermore, a critical examination is conducted of observable signs of interstellar panspermia, including the distribution of life-bearing comets and microbes found on planets, and it is discovered that even life transfer occurring in small star clusters remains difficult to detect. Nevertheless, the breakthrough in this research provides a framework that can be applied to a broader context, making it a valuable tool for studying and detecting life transfer in any situation.

Animal movement and population dynamics are interconnected, and modeling their connection can lead to a better understanding of conservation and management strategies. We developed a statistical model to analyze combined data from acoustic monitoring of bat movements and roosting choice surveys. This model simultaneously estimates the size of a bat population, identifies preferred roosting sites, and models population dynamics based on movement patterns within those sites. Our approach builds on the King's method of capture-recapture analysis and extends it to account for the selection of sites by incorporating a discrete logit model. This site-choice model acts as a detection probability model, with parameters estimated using Bayesian methods and a data augmentation approach. Our results show that the model can accurately estimate key population parameters with a slight overestimation of the standard error due to the complexity of the site-choice model. Furthermore, we found that a first-order autoregressive model adequately describes the population dynamics. This model has implications for the study of animal movements and can be applied to other contexts, such as whale movements tracked using acoustic recordings. In this work, we propose a straightforward parameterization strategy that utilizes a specific combination of the Cauchy stress operator's components, replacing the extensive nonlinear parametric formulation with a more manageable linear model. A key aspect of this approach is the utilization of specific constitutive operators that define material responses as reference baselines, allowing us to capture deviations from these standard behaviors rather than detailing the intricate dynamics of complex materials. As a result, this strategy enables the prediction of a broad spectrum of viscoelastic materials with significantly reduced parameterization, as demonstrated by our numerical examples. Additionally, this approach is computationally more efficient and aligns with the fundamental principles of thermodynamics, offering a reliable and simplified solution for modeling diverse viscoelastic materials.
