It argues that one key factor contributing to this outcome was the widespread use of a translation approach, which characterized the grid computing landscape. In effect, most participants in the grid community constructed their own individual grids rather than contributing to a unified whole. This phenomenon prevented a truly cohesive and inclusive grid from forming. The article also explores the implications of a prevailing translation culture for the development of complex technologies and societal systems. It suggests that a widespread reliance on translation practices can create obstacles to genuine integration and systemic change. We establish the convergence in distribution of the scaled local time of the simple random walk at a given level $x$ as the level $x$ tends to zero. The walk is assumed to be fair without drift, and we show that the pair of the second moment of the position and the local time at $x$ converges to a pair of independent random variables in a supercritical regime, where the scaling exponent $1/2$ is $2/3$ when the walk is unbiased, and $2$ when the walk is biased. When the walk is biased, we also consider the convergence of the local time to the product of the current position and the scaling factor. The results in this paper are a combination of existing findings by Mueller and Tribe, and new proofs that include biased walks. The approach used here is an extension of the method introduced by Shi and Yang. The tightness of the pair of the second moment of the position and the local time at $x$ is proven by using a new large deviation estimate for the local time at $x$, which can be of independent interest. The driving force behind this research was the desire to analyze the asymptotic behavior of the minimum of the local times at $x$, and to obtain this result we established the convergence in distribution of the scaled local time at $x$ along with the tightness of the pair of the second moment of the position and the local time at $x$. The approach used here can also be applied to other random walk models. The paper ends with an analysis of the maximum of the local times at $x$, the bias of the random walk with the maximum of the local times at $x$, and the distribution of the minimum of the local times at $x$. The results for the random walk can be generalized to random walks with drift. Understanding the intricate details of histopathology images is crucial for analyzing and diagnosing cancer. Accurate identification of nuclei within these images is a key step in this process. Due to the time-consuming and complex nature of manual nucleus segmentation, automating this process is vital. In response to this need, a growing trend in research has focused on developing techniques for automatic nucleus segmentation. However, the existing methods primarily concentrate on producing refined segmentations without giving much consideration to isolating individual nuclei. To address this shortfall, a new network called W-Net is proposed, specifically designed to extract nuclei while removing backgrounds and tumors from interest regions in gastro intestinal pathology images. W-Net consists of two main components: a feature extraction phase using a convolutional neural network, and a post-processing phase that refines the output through a convolutional neural network. To evaluate the network, experiments were conducted on a dataset consisting of gastro intestinal images, resulting in performance metrics of 0.783 for the IoU score and 0.821 for the F-score. The outstanding performance of W-Net was also verified by comparing it to the existing U-Net network. The pre-trained W-Net model is made available for download on the project website, along with instructions for implementing it in new projects. The development of W-Net highlights the potential for further improvements in nucleus segmentation, and encourages researchers to explore more comprehensive segmentation methods. The code for W-Net has been submitted to the GitHub platform, available at https://github.com/ghru/W-Net. The trained model is available for download at http://121.42.159.157/. The dataset used for training and testing the network is also available at http://121.42.159.157/. The project website is located at http://121.42.159.157/. The authors would like to express their gratitude to the anonymous reviewers for their feedback, and to Zhiyu Cheng, Yang Wang, and Boxuan Song for their contributions to the project. The project was conducted in collaboration with the Jiangsu University of Technology, the Nanjing Chengxiang Software Technology Co. Ltd, and the Jiangsu Province Cancer Hospital.

Building on the local exchange theorem for even classical groups from [1, 2], this study extends the result to include odd classical groups, specifically SO2n+1(q) and Sp2n+1(q), within the framework of characteristic p groups. The local exchange theorem enables a computation of the defect of the permutation branch in the Hecke correspondence for these odd classical groups, filling a gap in the literature and achieving the goal set forth in [1, 2]. Additionally, this research produces the desired result for Sp2n+1(q) in the missing case where n is even. The study also explores implications for the permutation branch's defect within the regime of the dual Weyl group, yielding a subclass of the inherited Coxeter graph structure. The underlying characteristic p setting creates specific challenges that require addressing the issue of missing information in the derived Bruhat order and developing a alternative, equivalent structure called the defect Bruhat order. The results obtained in this study are compared to their counterparts in the literature for the corresponding even classical groups in the framework of the dual Weyl group. The research also includes a notable result discovered during its course, specifically the equivalence between the defect and Bruhat orders. The study further provides several examples, including a notable one for the symplectic group Sp6(7), by constructing the Coxeter graph for the permutation branch's defect in the regime of the dual Weyl group. The research also explores the relationship between the Coxeter graph for the permutation branch's defect in the regime of the dual Weyl group and the Gelfand-Tetali inequality, leading to an inequality for the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomial associated with the defect Bruhat order. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex, irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A key discovery emerges from this examination, revealing that GCNNs can be viewed as a type of Residual Learning that seeks to model deviations from a well-fitting linear base model. A subsequent exploration of GCNN equivalents is carried out, revealing that they can be modified to handle multiple types of data by incorporating an additional learnable element. A numerical example serves to illustrate this concept, demonstrating that one form of GCNN can effectively be used to model non-linear relationships when operating with linear elements. A key limitation of GCNNs also emerges from this analysis, suggesting that they may struggle with inherently non-linear data sets. A related exploration of Linear Autoencoders is also presented, providing an innovative perspective on this established technique. A numerical assessment of various evaluation metrics for a model that has been subjected to an information injection attack on one of its input variables reveals that GCNNs generally perform poorly in such situations, with the exception of Mean Squared Error. A possible direction for future research on GCNNs is also proposed, encouraging the development of techniques that can detect and model non-linear relationships within data sets. A public implementation of the matched filtering GCNN framework, along with example code and datasets, is made available for download. A numerical assessment of different GCNN and graph autoencoder architectures is also carried out, with the results indicating that the information gained from the matched filtering analysis may not necessarily translate to better performance in comparison with other established techniques. A possible explanation for this is also presented, along with a proposal for further research on this topic. A related exploration of the Linear Projections technique is also conducted, with the results demonstrating that it is essentially equivalent to the matched filtering GCNN framework. A numerical assessment of the information gained from the matched filtering analysis of the Linear Projections technique is carried out, with the results indicating that it may provide a better performance in comparison with other established techniques in certain situations. A possible explanation for this is also presented, along with a proposal for further research on this topic. This results in the formation of solitons and black holes with unique hair structures. Specifically, solitons and soliton-like structures with soliton cores and mantle components can emerge when a specific potential is applied. Additionally, we find that uniform specific angular momentum accelerates the formation of solitons and rotating black hole structures with hair. Notably, the minimum angular momentum required to stabilize solitons and rotating black hole structures with hair decreases with increasing potential values. Furthermore, an examination of the solitons' and black hole's hair structures with respect to the Gauss law parameter, coupling constants, and mass parameters is conducted. The behavior of these structures is also compared with standard topological solitons. A key finding is that the solitons' and black hole's hair structures are identical to those found in the conventional topological solitons scenario. A key distinction, however, lies in the solitons' and black hole's hair structures' ability to dynamically change in response to changes in mass parameters, Gauss law parameter, and coupling constants. A soliton's mass parameter dependence on mass had been previously unreported and requires further investigation. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technology has sped up image acquisition, but its wide lateral coverage necessitates a precise method for estimating lateral shifts. Researchers have explored various techniques to determine this shift, with some using the virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) method, which employs a more precise estimation but is also more computationally intensive. Additionally, VSSA requires significant memory to function effectively. This paper presents an optimized virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) design, dubbed SA-light, which streamlines the process while maintaining comparable performance to the original VSSA design. SA-light reduces memory requirements by 95% while shortening processing time by 75%. This streamlined VSSA design also yields a more precise estimation of lateral shifts, outperforming the conventional method in 78% of cases. In line with the original VSSA design, SA-light exhibits superior performance in elastic image reconstruction, surpassing conventional SA design in 85% of cases. This optimized VSSA design is suited for use in elastography, an application that demands precise estimation of lateral shifts. In this context, SA-light reduces the dimension of the data matrix used for estimating lateral shifts, achieving this in 3 dimensions, as opposed to the original VSSA design that operates in 2 dimensions. This design also makes SA-light more lightweight, facilitating its integration into handheld ultrasound devices that employ VSSA technology. This device, in turn, features a sweep beamformer, an advancement over conventional devices that employ VSSA technology. In line with the original VSSA design, SA-light yields an image quality that is comparable to conventional SA design, as demonstrated in the analysis of the image quality metrics. In this context, SA-light yields an envelope pulse width that is 10% narrower than conventional SA design, an axial resolution that is 2% sharper than conventional SA design, an SNR that is 5% stronger than conventional SA design, an SID that is 8% better than conventional SA design, and an SIR that is 12% better than conventional SA design. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially function as a form of proofs with cut operations, thereby implicitly validating the rules they implement. This perspective enables us to reinterpret the structure of algorithms in terms of the proof principles they employ, based on their underlying logic. In particular, this relationship can be seen to reflect Godel's notion of "proofs as programs." Furthermore, it offers a fresh perspective on the concept of algorithm correctness, framing it in terms of the validity of the conclusions drawn from premises in accordance with the rules implemented in the algorithm. In essence, this viewpoint can be seen as a reexpression of the principle of "program correctness as proof," which underlies the basis of the Curry-Howard Letter and the Biscuit Project, among other related initiatives. This discussion is set within the broader context of the Curry-Howard Letter and the Biscuit Project, which seeks to explore the connection between imperative algorithms and logical proofs, specifically natural deduction. This connection can be visually represented by creating a map, or "landscape," of these algorithms in terms of their underlying proof principles. Such a landscape may serve as a platform for identifying algorithms that are equivalent in terms of their structure, as well as those that, when combined, correspond to valid proofs that can be verified through natural deduction. This discussion is further illustrated with a concrete example, namely the algorithm for combining vectors in the GLM library, which is shown to be equivalent to a natural deduction rule governing the same operation. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale stochastic chase-evasion games on grid worlds by dividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach involves a high-level decision-making process for nodal behavior and a set of lower-level 'child' agents, each associated with a specific grid node, making independent decisions to navigate their surrounding micro-environments. We developed a two-stage resolution process, starting with a coarse-grained analysis of the game using the macro-states and subsequently refining the assessment with the child agents at the individual node level. By establishing connections to existing methods, we show that our hierarchical framework encompasses non-hierarchical strategies and other combinatorial solution techniques. Furthermore, our model enables efficient performance compared to unHierarchical methods. We demonstrated our approach's effectiveness through large-scale grid world chase-evasion scenarios. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/andrew-kimber/hierarchies.

The Vector Boson Approximation efficiently models high-energy electron-proton collisions, 
however its applicability is limited to high energies. A refined version of VBA, 
extending its validity to lower energies, is developed and the approximations' 
validity are defined by specific criteria. The updated VBA maintains the efficiency 
of the original version while accurately describing low-energy interactions and is 
particularly beneficial for muon colliders where incoming beams have limited energy. 
The VBA framework includes corrections addressing radiation effects and allows for 
the inclusion of non-radiative initial state effects, further enhancing its precision. 
The updated VBA is suitable for the majority of small-angle processes at muon colliders.

future high-energy muon colliders, is also explored. The VBA's implementation in 
the form of the Efficient Vector Boson Approximation (EVBA) code is publicly available.

We develop a formal proof for the statement "Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser worked at the University of California, Berkeley". Our investigation into their careers is carried out within the formal proof assistant Lean, utilizing the library "mathlib" which is comprised of mathematical theorems and proofs. We break down the process of verifying their affiliation with Berkeley in two parts: first, we establish the fact that each of them worked at Berkeley within the "mathlib" library, and second, we provide a formal proof for this fact. Additionally, we create a formal proof for the incorrect assertion "5 is a prime number", demonstrating the capability to efficiently generate flawed proofs in an automated manner. By exploring the structure of "mathlib" through example proofs, this work aims to guide users through developing a deeper understanding of the contents of "mathlib" and provide a foundation for creating custom extensions to the library.

This paper formulates two versions of the three balls conjecture in Clifford analysis, one for eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator and another more general one. We then provide a specific scenario where the first version of the three balls conjecture holds, and it's shown that the second version of the three balls conjecture is a consequence of the first one. Additionally, we offer some estimates for a broader class of functions that include the eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator. These estimates are derived from a mean value theorem applied to the second version of the three balls conjecture. The research also explores and generalizes a result found in "The three balls conjecture for harmonic functions in $\mathbb{R}^n$" by A. Henrot and C. Kumar. The paper ultimately concludes with some open problems related to the two versions of the three balls conjecture in Clifford analysis. In solving inverse problems, a conditional GAN can be utilized to generate a plausible image that represents the problem's underlying reality, given the observed and flawed data as input. This generated image corresponds to a specific posterior probability in the problem's uncertainty domain. However, having multiple such plausible images exists, making it difficult to determine if they indeed stem from the same posterior distribution. To address this issue, we propose a new conditional GAN, postered, which is designed to output a probability distribution that accurately reflects the uncertainty in the inverse problem. postered includes a unique mechanism for generating multiple distinct probability distributions, each corresponding to a different possible posterior, and incorporates three distinct regularization techniques - spectral normalization, adversarial training, and maximum likelihood estimation - to ensure these distributions are legitimate, diverse, and accurately capture the uncertainty in the inverse problem. By training the model using a combination of an inverse problem and an overparameterized deep linear regression problem, we demonstrate its effectiveness in postered, showing that the model's output distributions successfully capture the uncertainty in the inverse problem. Additionally, we show that the model's performance can be further improved when the input data has an implanted perturbation. Finally, we apply postered to real-world image deblurring problems and compare its performance with existing methods, showing its superiority in recovering clean images. We establish the impossibility of creating invariant surfaces in dynamical systems driven by fractional-order differential equations, given specific system configurations. These conditions are characterized, and our findings are further illustrated with numerical examples. Additionally, we demonstrate that fractional-order surface invariant properties are unlikely in certain specialized scenarios, including those with constant coefficients and systems defined by certain fractional differential equations without coefficients. The unlikely nature of surface invariant properties in other scenarios, such as those with the Caputo fractional derivative, is also highlighted. Our approach to achieving these results involves applying a recently introduced fractional-order version of the Lyapunov matrix equation, as well as a stability matrix equation driven by fractional-order differential equations, to investigate the surface stability and expand the definition of surface stability to include all possible surface types.
